Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles

Wang Ma Debarun Bhattacharjya Junkyu Lee Affiliation: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute  Lirio  IBM Software Innovation Lab Email: nhan.ph0407@gmail.com    Nhan H. Pham Harsha Kokel Qiang Ji Affiliation: Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute  Lirio  IBM Software Innovation Lab Affiliation: Independent Researcher{maw6, jiq}@rpi.edu, dbhattacharjya@lirio.com, Junkyu.Lee@ibm.com, Email: harsha.kokel@ibm.com
Abstract

Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

11footnotetext: This work was done while Wang Ma was an intern, and Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H. Pham, and Harsha Kokel were researchers, at IBM Research.††footnotetext: Code: https://github.com/wma17/Black-box_UQ_for_LLMs_Ensemble_of_Ensemble

1 Introduction & Related Work

Large language models (LLMs) are widely deployed in search, code assistance, and scientific workflows, where uncertainty quantification (UQ) helps detect hallucinations and guide abstention. Crucially, when an LLM is uncertain, the appropriate action depends on why: an ambiguous query calls for clarification, whereas a knowledge gap calls for retrieval or deferral. Existing black-box UQ methods, however, collapse output variability into a single consistency score that flags unreliability without diagnosing its source. We disentangle these two sources from black-box sampled generations via a two-level ensemble with exact finite-sample bias correction.

From Bayesian UQ to black-box LLMs. Bayesian neural networks [12] and deep ensembles [26] give a principled aleatoric/epistemic split via the law of total variance, but exact or approximate inference over billions of parameters is intractable for modern LLMs, where deployment often offers only black-box sampling access.

Related work. LLM-UQ divides into two strands: white-box methods that exploit logits, hidden states, or trained heads to score semantic uncertainty or detect hallucinations [22, 10, 24, 11], and black-box methods that infer uncertainty from behavioral variability across samples without internal access [35, 13, 58, 59, 4]; surveys offer broader context [57, 33]. A growing line of semantic-aware black-box scorers sharpens semantic entropy via kernel-, graph-, or volume-based objects on response embeddings [38, 37, 61, 29, 41]. Concurrent AU/EU-split attempts for LLMs use trained clarification heads, spectral decompositions, variational ICL, paraphrase prompting, or conformal coverage [16, 52, 19, 6, 40]. These works share our goal but emit a single scalar or are structurally one-level (perturbations or decoding, not both), so they cannot expose the AU/EU split our two-level construction targets. The closest perturbation-based black-box method is SPUQ [13], which perturbs prompts but is one-level and reports a scalar consistency score. Outside the LLM setting, Wang and Ji [53] argued from a first-order optimization view that local input perturbations approximate parameter perturbations for pre-trained vision models; we adapt that intuition to LLMs and turn it from heuristic motivation into an explicit AU/EU approximation bound for a nested estimator (Thm. 4.2; App. A.3). Our two-level construction is what enables both the AU/EU split (Sec. 4.1) and the separation from consistency-only UQ that fixed-prompt methods provably cannot exhibit (Sec. 4.3).

Contributions. We move black-box LLM-UQ beyond a scalar consistency score: our two-level ensemble (Fig. 1) admits an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition of embedded-generation covariance to estimate AU and EU, and we equip the decomposition with theory that makes it both estimable and falsifiable. Concretely:

  1. 1.

    Exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition with finite-MM bias correction for AU/EU estimation. An exact within-/between-perturbation split of embedded-generation covariance, plus a closed-form bias correction that makes the epistemic estimator unbiased at any inner sample size M≥2M\!\geq\!2 (Sec. 4.1).

  2. 2.

    Bayesian bridge to parameter-posterior AU/EU with diagnostic conditions. Defect bounds connecting perturbation-population AU/EU to Bayesian AU/EU through three local conditions that we estimate as diagnostics from the same outputs the estimator already collects (Sec. 4.2).

  3. 3.

    Provable separation from consistency-only UQ. A class of failures any consistency-only method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects; in paired interventions, prompt clarification significantly reduces EU while leaving fixed-prompt baselines unchanged (Sec. 4.3, 5.4).

  4. 4.

    Empirical results. On five short-form QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, the estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines (Sec. 5.2); at a matched generation budget, it matches leading one-level black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU (Sec. 5.3); paired interventions on AmbigQA and Natural Questions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure (Sec. 5.4); the predicted finite-MM bias correction is verified empirically (Sec. 5.5); a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining (Sec. 5.6); and ablations confirm stability under embedding choice and sampling budget (Sec. 5.7).

2 Background

Bayesian uncertainty decomposition. Bayesian neural networks [14, 12] treat parameters θ\theta as random variables with posterior p⁡(θ∣D)p(\theta\mid D), yielding a predictive p⁡(y∣x,D)=𝔼p⁡(θ∣D)​[p⁡(y∣x,θ)]p(y\mid x,D)=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid D)}[p(y\mid x,\theta)] that decomposes total predictive uncertainty into aleatoric (irreducible data/decoding noise) and epistemic (reducible model knowledge) components [23, 18, 8]. For continuous outputs parameterized by (μθ​(x),σθ2​(x))(\mu_{\theta}(x),\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(x)) [2],

AU=𝔼p⁡(θ∣D)​[σθ2​(x)],EU=Varp⁡(θ∣D)​[μθ​(x)],TU=AU+EU.\mathrm{AU}=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid D)}[\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(x)],\hskip 9.24994pt\mathrm{EU}=\mathrm{Var}_{p(\theta\mid D)}[\mu_{\theta}(x)],\hskip 9.24994pt\mathrm{TU}=\mathrm{AU}+\mathrm{EU}.

This regression form is the conceptual target we adapt: we replace scalar mean/variance with embedding-space mean/covariance so the same identity applies to free-form generation, and we replace the parameter posterior (intractable for billion-parameter LLMs) with a perturbation distribution we can sample from.

Input perturbation as a black-box surrogate. Direct sampling from p⁡(θ∣D)p(\theta\mid D) is infeasible for pre-trained black-box LLMs. As a methodological motivation, the local equivalence of Wang and Ji [53] (Prop. 3.3) approximates small parameter variations by structured input-embedding perturbations: f⁡(x+Δ​x,θ)≈f⁡(x,θ+Δ​θ)f(x{+}\Delta x,\theta)\approx f(x,\theta{+}\Delta\theta), so input perturbations induce output changes similar to those a small parameter perturbation would induce. We treat this as a proxy for p⁡(y∣x,D)p(y\mid x,D) at fixed parameters: input perturbations serve as a tractable surrogate for an intractable parameter posterior. The exact relationship is deferred to Thm. 4.2 (Sec. 4.2), which formalizes the local conditions and bounds the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian AU/EU. Throughout, we operate on three distinct objects: a Bayesian target, an operational perturbation-population quantity, and a finite-sample estimator; the estimator we build in Sec. 3 is defined in perturbation-population terms, and the Bayesian interpretation is established under the local bridge conditions of Sec. 4.2.

3 Proposed Method: Uncertainty Quantification via Ensemble-of-Ensembles

We propose a two-level black-box UQ framework for LLMs that requires neither retraining nor access to token-level logits. An outer ensemble draws meaning-preserving semantic perturbations Δ∼pΔ\Delta\!\sim\!p_{\Delta} of the input xx, yielding xΔ:=T⁡(x,Δ)x_{\Delta}\!:=\!T(x,\Delta); an inner ensemble draws stochastic decodes Y∼p(⋅∣xΔ)Y\!\sim\!p(\cdot\!\mid\!x_{\Delta}) at fixed deployed parameters θ⋆\theta^{\star}. We measure variability in a sentence-embedding space Z=e⁡(Y)∈ℝdZ=e(Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (assume 𝔼​‖Z‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|Z\|^{2}<\infty), where the law of total covariance gives

Cov⁡(Z)⏟UT​(x)=𝔼Δ​[Cov⁡(Z∣Δ)]⏟UA​(x)​(within-perturbation)+CovΔ⁡(𝔼⁡[Z∣Δ])⏟UE​(x)​(between-perturbation).\underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}(Z)}_{U_{T}(x)}=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}[\operatorname{Cov}(Z\!\mid\!\Delta)]}_{U_{A}(x)\;\text{(within-perturbation)}}+\underbrace{\operatorname{Cov}_{\Delta}(\mathbb{E}[Z\!\mid\!\Delta])}_{U_{E}(x)\;\text{(between-perturbation)}}. (1)

We adopt Eq. (1) as the definition of the perturbation-population uncertainties (UA,UE,UT)≡(𝒰AΔ,𝒰EΔ,𝒰TΔ)(U_{A},U_{E},U_{T})\equiv(\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta},\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta},\mathcal{U}_{T}^{\Delta}). The interpretation mirrors the Bayesian split: UAU_{A} aggregates within-perturbation variability (decoding stochasticity at a fixed prompt and ambiguity in the prompt itself), while UEU_{E} measures between-perturbation disagreement of conditional means, i.e. how much the model’s expected behavior changes under semantically equivalent phrasings. The corresponding Bayesian targets and finite-sample estimators are formally distinguished in Sec. 4.2 (full definitions in App. A.3.1; summary in App. Tab. 8). Fig. 1 summarizes the full pipeline; pseudocode is in App. Alg. 1.

Outer ensemble: meaning-preserving perturbations. We obtain NN semantically equivalent variants {x1,…,xN}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\} of xx by a two-stage localized procedure adapted from Hu et al. [17]: its embedding-space nearest-neighbor step provides the locality our Bayesian bridge (Sec. 4.2) requires.

Stage 1 (offline, once per dataset). An auxiliary paraphraser produces a pool 𝒫x={xk′}k=1Kpool\mathcal{P}_{x}=\{x^{\prime}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{pool}}} for each input xx; we cache its embeddings {e⁡(xk′)}k=1Kpool\{e(x^{\prime}_{k})\}_{k=1}^{K_{\mathrm{pool}}}.

Stage 2 (online, per query). For i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N we sample isotropic Gaussian noise in embedding space and snap to the nearest cached paraphrase:

δi∼𝒩⁡(0,ε2​Id),xi=arg⁡minxk′∈𝒫x⁡D⁡(e⁡(x)+δi,e⁡(xk′)),\delta_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\varepsilon^{2}I_{d}),\qquad x_{i}\;=\;\arg\min_{x^{\prime}_{k}\in\mathcal{P}_{x}}\;D\!\big(e(x)+\delta_{i},\;e(x^{\prime}_{k})\big), (2)

where D⁡(⋅,⋅)D(\cdot,\cdot) is cosine distance. Since N≪KpoolN\!\ll\!K_{\mathrm{pool}}, this draws a localized neighborhood rather than enumerating the pool. The hyperparameters (Kpool,ε)(K_{\mathrm{pool}},\varepsilon) trade off locality (staying inside a region where the bridge linearization is plausible) and coverage (paraphrase diversity); both are ablated in App. F. The AU/EU split is robust across perturbation families: random paraphrasing and SPUQ-style noise both yield meaningful AU/EU under the two-level pipeline (App. Tab. 24).

Inner ensemble: stochastic decoding. For each xix_{i} we draw MM stochastic decodes {yi,j}j=1M∼p(⋅∣xi)\{y_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{M}\!\sim\!p(\cdot\!\mid\!x_{i}) under fixed sampling temperature, and embed them as zi,j=e⁡(yi,j)z_{i,j}=e(y_{i,j}). The per-prompt sample mean and covariance are

μ^i=1M​∑j=1Mzi,j,Σ^i=1M−1​∑j=1M(zi,j−μ^i)​(zi,j−μ^i)⊤.\hat{\mu}_{i}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}z_{i,j},\qquad\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{M-1}\sum_{j=1}^{M}(z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})(z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})^{\top}. (3)

Two-level estimators and bias correction. Aggregating across the outer ensemble gives the empirical AU and (raw) EU estimators

𝒰^A​(x)=1N​∑i=1NΣ^i,𝒰^Eraw​(x)=1N−1​∑i=1N(μ^i−μ¯)​(μ^i−μ¯)⊤,μ¯=1N​∑iμ^i.\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{A}(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}(x)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat{\mu}_{i}-\bar{\mu})(\hat{\mu}_{i}-\bar{\mu})^{\top},\hskip 9.24994pt\bar{\mu}=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\hat{\mu}_{i}. (4)

Because μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} is itself an MM-sample average, 𝒰^Eraw\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}} absorbs an 1M\tfrac{1}{M} leakage from 𝒰^A\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{A} (Prop. 4.1); we therefore use the bias-corrected estimator throughout,

𝒰^E​(x)=𝒰^Eraw​(x)−1M​𝒰^A​(x),𝒰^T​(x)=𝒰^A​(x)+𝒰^E​(x).\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{E}(x)\;=\;\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}(x)\;-\;\tfrac{1}{M}\,\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{A}(x),\hskip 18.49988pt\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{T}(x)\;=\;\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{A}(x)+\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{E}(x). (5)

For correctness ranking we reduce each d×dd{\times}d matrix to a scalar by the trace, u∙​(x)=tr⁡(𝒰^∙​(x))u_{\bullet}(x)=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\widehat{\mathcal{U}}_{\bullet}(x)\big); mean, max, and sum reductions are ablated in App. F. Per-query cost is N​MNM LLM decodes plus a one-time paraphrase pool of size KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}} amortized across the dataset, and can be reduced via per-query adaptive stopping (App. F.1.2). Throughout the paper, KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}} refers exclusively to this offline pool; it is distinct from the perturbation count of one-level baselines.

4 Theoretical Results

We establish three theoretical results: (i) an exact finite-MM bias identity and concentration bound for the perturbation-population estimators (Pillar 1, Sec. 4.1); (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap to parameter-posterior AU/EU via three data-estimable local diagnostics (Pillar 2, Sec. 4.2); and (iii) a separation theorem characterizing failure modes that fixed-prompt consistency methods provably miss (Pillar 3, Sec. 4.3); proofs in App. A.

4.1 Pillar 1: bias-corrected finite-MM estimator

Estimating UA,UEU_{A},U_{E} from NN outer perturbations and MM inner decodes per perturbation introduces a structural bias: the naive epistemic estimator absorbs 1M\tfrac{1}{M} of the aleatoric covariance.

Proposition 4.1 (Finite-MM bias of the epistemic estimator; informal).

The naive estimator U^Eraw\widehat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}} obtained as the sample covariance of inner means is biased upward by exactly 1M​𝒰AΔ​(x)\tfrac{1}{M}\,\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x) relative to the perturbation-population EU, while U^A(M)\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)} is unbiased. The corrected estimator U^E(M):=U^Eraw−1M​U^A(M)\widehat{U}_{E}^{(M)}:=\widehat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}-\tfrac{1}{M}\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)} is unbiased and concentrates at O⁡(log⁡(1/δ)/N)O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/N}) plus lower-order 1/M1/M terms. Formal statement, constants, and proof in App. A.2 (Prop. A.1, Thm. A.5).

The leakage is empirically large at small MM: ρ⁡(U^A,U^Eraw)=0.65\rho(\widehat{U}_{A},\widehat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}){=}0.65 at M=3M{=}3 on TriviaQA, and the closed-form correction—a single matrix subtraction—drives it to 0.120.12 at the same budget (Sec. 5.5, Tab. 5).

4.2 Pillar 2: Bayesian bridge with diagnostic conditions

The targets here are the Bayesian AU/EU 𝒰ABayes​(x):=𝔼θ​[Σθ​(x)]\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x){:=}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\Sigma_{\theta}(x)], 𝒰EBayes​(x):=Covθ​(mθ​(x))\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x){:=}\mathrm{Cov}_{\theta}(m_{\theta}(x)) defined over a parameter posterior p⁡(θ∣𝒟)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D}): the ground truth Bayesian UQ ultimately seeks. Pillar 1 bounds the (estimator)→\to(perturbation-population) gap from Eq. (1); the bridge below bounds the (perturbation-population)→\to(Bayesian) gap; composing the two yields an end-to-end bound (formal definitions of the three flavors collected in App. A.3.1; proofs in App. A.3).

Theorem 4.2 (Bayesian bridge for perturbation AU/EU; informal).

Under three local conditions on the model around xx (first-order linearity of the conditional mean, locally Gaussian posterior, and bounded semantic coverage defect), the bias-corrected estimators of Pillar 1 satisfy

‖U^A(M)​(x)−𝒰ABayes​(x)‖F≤MC error⏟O⁡(log⁡(1/δ)/N)+εA​(x)⏟bridge defect,\big\|\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)}(x)-\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)\big\|_{F}\;\leq\;\underbrace{\text{MC error}}_{O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/N})}\;+\;\underbrace{\varepsilon_{A}(x)}_{\text{bridge defect}},

and analogously for U^E(M)\widehat{U}_{E}^{(M)}. The defects εA,εE\varepsilon_{A},\varepsilon_{E} shrink with the three conditions; precise statement, assumptions, and proof are in App. A.3 (Thms. A.10, A.12).

The two model-side conditions align with existing LLM theory: local first-order linearity matches the regime of linear-probing-then-fine-tuning [51], and the locally-Gaussian posterior is the Laplace approximation standard in the Bayesian-LoRA line [60]. We further measure each defect from outputs the estimator already collects: D1, an OLS residual of μΔ​(x)\mu_{\Delta}(x) on Δ\Delta (local linearity); D2, a Henze–Zirkler statistic on the embedding clouds (local Gaussianity); D3, an MMD between the perturbation cloud and a held-out semantic reference (distributional coverage). Per-dataset values are in App. C (Tab. 12). Consistent with first-order scaling, sweeping ε∈[0.01,0.2]\varepsilon\in[0.01,0.2] induces a nearly linear rise in EU (R2=0.978R^{2}{=}0.978) while AU shifts by 2.3%2.3\% (App. F.2.1); instruction perturbations similarly act as implicit parameter updates under the dual gradient view of ICL [7] (App. D).

4.3 Pillar 3: provable separation from consistency-only UQ

Theorem 4.3 (Perturbation–consistency separation; informal).

Let ℱcons\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cons}} be any uncertainty estimator that depends only on repeated decoding at a fixed prompt (e.g., 54, 35, 24; SPUQ 13 is not in this class because it perturbs the prompt before decoding). On the class of inputs where decoding is effectively deterministic but μΔ​(x)\mu_{\Delta}(x) varies non-trivially across semantic-preserving perturbations, ℱcons​(x)=0\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cons}}(x)\!=\!0 while perturbation EU is bounded away from zero. The class has positive measure whenever the model has prompt-format-driven outputs. Formal statement and construction in App. A.4.

Confident hallucinations, memorized templates, and prompt-format artifacts produce stable outputs at a fixed prompt, so any consistency-only score is exactly zero on them while perturbation EU remains positive. In Sec. 5.4, disambiguating a prompt significantly reduces EU while leaving all fixed-prompt baselines unchanged (Tab. 5).

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental setup

Experiment roadmap. We organize the experiments around six questions. (Q1) Under the standard UQ protocol, do our uncertainty scores rank incorrect answers above correct ones? (§5.2, Tab. 1) (Q2) At a matched budget, how does two-level sampling compare with one-level designs? (§5.3, Tab. 2) (Q3) Beyond correctness prediction, do AU and EU respond to different actionable sources of failure? (§5.4, Tabs. 3, 5) (Q4) Does the finite-MM bias correction predicted by Prop. 4.1 behave as the theory predicts? (§5.5, Tab. 5) (Q5) Does the framework extend beyond short-form answers to claim-level long-form factuality? (§5.6, Tab. 6) (Q6) Are the conclusions stable under key design choices such as the embedding backbone and the two-level sampling budget? (§5.7, Tab. 7)

Tasks and datasets. We evaluate black-box uncertainty estimation on five short-form QA benchmarks: TriviaQA [21] (no-context), TruthfulQA [31], GPQA [46], SciQA [3], and CoQA [44]; we also include AmbigQA [36] and Natural Questions [25] for the paired AU/EU interventions in §5.4, and the NQ long-answer split for the long-form pilot in §5.6. The goal is to test whether uncertainty reliably predicts answer correctness.

Models. We use four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales: LLaMA-3-70B, LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Qwen2.5-7B [15, 43]. The main paper presents the smaller two (LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) in Tab. 1; 70B/72B results are in App. Tab. 17.

Correctness labeling. Two complementary automatic criteria: (1) Cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of generated vs. reference answers (threshold >0.8>0.8), and (2) ROUGE-L overlap (threshold >0.5>0.5) [45, 30]. Both criteria are reported to reduce metric-specific artifacts. In §5.3 and App. F.2.3, we additionally evaluate under Exact Match (EM) on TriviaQA as an encoder-independent correctness criterion.

Uncertainty measures. We report AUROC for correctness prediction using aleatoric (AU), epistemic (EU), and total uncertainty (TU) as defined in Eq. (1); following the UQ convention, the positive class is incorrect and the scoring signal is the (uncorrected sign) uncertainty value, so AUROC measures how well higher uncertainty ranks errors above correct answers.

Baselines. Black-box: D-SE [24], Self-Consistency [54], SIMBA [4], SelfCheckGPT [35], SPUQ [13], and a P(True) probe [22]. White-box: G-NLL [1], PE / LN-PE [34], and SE / LN-SE [11, 24]. The long-form pilot (§5.6) additionally compares against five long-form-specific scorers from Bouchard et al. [5]: avgEntail, NonContradiction, UQLM cosine, plus SelfCheckGPT and ROUGE-L (cons.) at long-form. Full baseline configurations are in App. H; SPUQ uses its three perturbation modes with KSPUQ=10K_{\mathrm{SPUQ}}{=}10 perturbations (SPUQ’s perturbation count, distinct from our offline pool size KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}}; KSPUQK_{\mathrm{SPUQ}} plays the role of our outer count NN) and pairwise ROUGE-L aggregation [13] (see App. D).

Sampling budget. For the headline AUROC table (Tab. 1) we use N=M=20N{=}M{=}20 (budget ablation in App. F.1); the AU/EU validation experiments (§5.4) and all other ablations use the compute-efficient default N=M=10N{=}M{=}10, and the long-form pilot (§5.6) uses the further-reduced N=M=5N{=}M{=}5 for efficiency over a separately-extracted claim set (see App. E). When comparing to SPUQ in App. D, we match the outer perturbation count (KSPUQ=N=10K_{\mathrm{SPUQ}}{=}N{=}10); our method then incurs the additional cost of an inner ensemble (MM stochastic decodes per perturbation) which is intrinsic to the two-level decomposition and not present in any one-level baseline. Per-method per-question call counts and wall-clock times are tabulated in App. Tab. 20.

Other settings. Decoding temperature TT is treated as an internal property of the deployed LLM, not an estimator knob: a targeted T-sweep (App. F.7) shows EU AUROC stable across T∈[0.3,1.5]T\!\in\![0.3,1.5]. The perturbation noise scale ε=0.1\varepsilon{=}0.1 comes from the noise-level ablation (App. F.2.1); the paraphrase pool size is Kpool=500K_{\mathrm{pool}}{=}500 for short-form QA (the ablation in App. Tab. 30 shows Kpool∈[20,100]K_{\mathrm{pool}}{\in}[20,100] is also competitive).

5.2 Headline AUROC: short-form correctness prediction

Tab. 1 reports correctness-prediction AUROC against strong white-box and black-box baselines under the standard protocol; the behavioral semantics of the AU/EU split are tested in §5.4.

(i) AU and TU are the strongest black-box signals overall, competitive with white-box methods that require token logits: AU reaches 0.8450.845/0.8150.815 under ROUGE-L on TriviaQA (LLaMA-3-8B / Qwen2.5-7B), the best black-box score in both columns, and AU or TU achieves the best black-box score in 1212 and the best overall score in 1111 of 2020 benchmark×\timescorrectness×\timesmodel cells.

(ii) AU is robust where prior black-box baselines collapse: on TruthfulQA, SPUQ (≤0.602\leq 0.602) and SIMBA on LLaMA-3-8B (≤0.520\leq 0.520) drift toward chance while AU remains informative.

(iii) EU contributes a complementary signal. EU targets knowledge-gap detection rather than generic correctness ranking, as validated by paired intervention in Tab. 3; on Qwen2.5-7B / GPQA / ROUGE-L it is the single best score across all methods (0.9490.949), and on the three hard benchmarks (GPQA, SciQA, CoQA) AU and EU together hold the top black-box position in 5/125/12 Cos/R-L columns. The 70B/72B counterpart on TriviaQA (App. Tab. 17) extends the same pattern.

5.3 Matched-budget comparison against one-level designs

Tab. 2 fixes the per-question generation budget B∈{10,25,100}B\!\in\!\{10,25,100\} across 400400 TriviaQA questions per model (EM labels) and compares alternative allocations: all BB decodes at the original prompt (fixed prompt); one decode per paraphrase across BB paraphrases (perturbation-only, N=BN{=}B, M=1M{=}1); an equal split between the two with summed variances (decoupled); SPUQ; Semantic Density [42]; and our nested estimator with N×M=5×2N{\times}M{=}5{\times}2, 5×55{\times}5, and 10×1010{\times}10.

(i) Competitive error ranking with an explicit AU/EU split. At every budget BB, SPUQ, fixed-prompt embedding variance, and our AU lie within 0.040.04 AUROC of one another with overlapping 95%95\% CIs (our TU is within 0.010.01–0.030.03 on LLaMA-3-8B and 0.040.04–0.070.07 on Qwen2.5-7B of the top black-box score), matching one-level error ranking while decomposing AU and EU.

(ii) Stability across budgets. Our AU and TU vary by less than 0.030.03 across all budgets BB. By contrast, perturbation-only (N=B,M=1N{=}B,M{=}1) drops from 0.7540.754 to 0.6670.667 on LLaMA-3-8B and from 0.7430.743 to 0.5530.553 on Qwen2.5-7B between B=10B{=}10 and 2525, as M=1M{=}1 lacks inner averaging and draws from an extended paraphrase pool at B≥25B{\geq}25 (App. F.1.1).

(iii) Semantic Density. Our AU outperforms uniform Semantic Density in every column, whereas the likelihood-weighted variant leads on Qwen2.5-7B at B≥25B{\geq}25 by utilizing white-box token probabilities.

5.4 Behavioral validation of the AU/EU split

We test the AU/EU split behaviorally with a 2×22{\times}2 paired-intervention protocol that targets one source of uncertainty at a time, directly probing the actionability of the decomposition—a property correctness-prediction AUROC alone cannot reveal. All experiments use LLaMA-3-8B with N=M=10N{=}M{=}10 on 1,0001{,}000 examples (Qwen2.5-7B replication in App. B). The paired statistic differences the per-example AUROC contribution between treatment and control, yielding a Wald zz-test for the contrast Δ​AU−Δ​EU\Delta\mathrm{AU}-\Delta\mathrm{EU} (or its twin).

Paired interventions (2×22{\times}2). On AmbigQA [36], adding a gold clarification removes ambiguity; on Natural Questions [25], adding the gold evidence passage closes the knowledge gap (perturbations applied only to the question, not the passage). The framework predicts clarification moves AU more than EU, and evidence moves EU more than AU. Tab. 3 confirms both: the contrast is significant in every cell (p<0.01p{<}0.01), and the absolute change on the predicted-target head is about 22–4×4{\times} the change on the off-target head in every row.

Score-level shifts and fixed-prompt baselines. Whereas Tab. 3 evaluates discriminative error-ranking gains (Δ​AUROC\Delta\text{AUROC}), Tab. 5 measures standardized shifts in raw uncertainty magnitude under both interventions across our three components, four fixed-prompt baselines, and SPUQ (LLaMA-3-8B, 1010 decodes per baseline; App. B).

Supplying evidence on NQ significantly reduces uncertainty across all methods except uniform Semantic Density. By contrast, clarifying the prompt on AmbigQA significantly reduces only the perturbation-sensitive scores—EU (−0.218-0.218), TU (−0.156-0.156), and SPUQ (−0.106-0.106)—while all fixed-prompt baselines remain statistically unchanged, corroborating Thm. 4.3.

Because SPUQ emits a single scalar that drops under both interventions, it cannot distinguish prompt ambiguity from missing knowledge. Our decomposition separates the two: clarification resolves cross-paraphrase divergence over competing interpretations (lowering EU magnitude in Tab. 5) while sharpening within-prompt variance to better rank residual errors (Δ​AU=+0.058\Delta\mathrm{AU}{=}{+}0.058, Tab. 3).

5.5 Empirical validation of the finite-MM bias correction

The behavioral test above uses the bias-corrected EU estimator. We next verify that the correction predicted by Prop. 4.1 is empirically necessary and behaves as the theory predicts (Tab. 5). The naive estimator inflates EU by 1M​UA\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A}, so the raw AU–EU correlation should start high at small MM and converge from above to the corrected correlation as 1/M→01/M\!\to\!0.

On TriviaQA (LLaMA-3-8B, Cosine, N=10N{=}10) the gap shrinks monotonically from 0.5320.532 at M=3M{=}3 to 0.0700.070 at M=30M{=}30 (Tab. 5); TruthfulQA shrinks identically (→0.0900.474\!\to\!0.090 for M=→20M{=}3\!\to\!20). The same shrinkage replicates on Qwen2.5-7B and across both datasets: at the level of the raw uncertainty scores themselves, the mean raw-vs-corrected EU gap shrinks by roughly an order of magnitude from M=3M{=}3 to M=30M{=}30 in every cell of the full {\{LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B}×{\}\times\{TriviaQA, TruthfulQA}\} grid (and across both Cosine and ROUGE-L correctness criteria), matching the 1M\tfrac{1}{M} rate predicted by Prop. 4.1 and confirming the correction is model- and dataset-invariant.

5.6 Beyond short-form: long-form pilot on NQ Long-Answer

Short-answer QA gives clean correctness labels but tests only one slice of LLM use. To check that the framework extends to long-form generation, we apply our two-level estimator to the NQ long-answer split [25] via segment-level decomposition: each generated long answer is split into atomic claims, each claim is scored independently with our two-level pipeline, and the resulting per-claim score is correlated with a per-claim factuality label (LLM judge). We compare against five published long-form-specific black-box baselines: avgEntail, NonContradiction [5], UQLM cosine [47], SelfCheckGPT [35], and ROUGE-L (cons.) [30]; baselines and our method draw from the same inner-sample pool (MM stochastic decodes at the unperturbed prompt) so the consistency-only comparators see exactly the budget our inner level sees.

Tab. 6 reports the claim-level result on LLaMA-3-8B (n=1,104n{=}1{,}104 claims) and Qwen2.5-7B (n=872n{=}872 claims).

(i) Ours (AU) is the second-best AUROC method on both models, within 0.0090.009 of avgEntail on LLaMA-3-8B and 0.0600.060 on Qwen2.5-7B, where avgEntail leverages a pretrained NLI classifier tailored to claim entailment.

(ii) The AU >> EU ordering is preserved at long-form, mirroring the short-form result.

(iii) We outperform surface-similarity baselines (SelfCheckGPT, ROUGE-L (cons.)) on both models. The two-level structure transports cleanly to claim-level long-form factuality without retraining; combining our perturbation outer level with NLI-based inner aggregation is a natural extension. The response-level companion table is in App. E.

5.7 Ablation studies

We ablate five orthogonal axes; our primary findings hold across all of them. The two most central axes are summarized in Tab. 7: the embedding backbone (panel a) and the two-level sampling budget (panel b). The remaining axes (noise magnitude ε\varepsilon, perturbation mechanism, vector-to-scalar aggregation, and paraphrase pool size KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}}) are in App. F.

(1) Embedding backbone: AU is encoder-stable in absolute level and rank-stable per-example. Re-encoding the same generations under three off-the-shelf sentence encoders (Sentence-BERT [45], MPNet, BGE-base) yields AU AUROC spreads of ≤0.05\leq 0.05 within every (model, dataset) cell, worst-case 0.0450.045 on LLaMA-3-8B / TruthfulQA (Tab. 7(a)). The stronger statement is on per-example ranks: pairwise Spearman correlations of AU scores across encoders are at least 0.9550.955 in every cell. A downstream consumer of our scores (abstention thresholds, selective evaluation) gets nearly the same ranking regardless of encoder choice; both axes extend across both correctness criteria (spread at most 0.0530.053 under ROUGE-L; App. Tab. 28). Different encoders agree on which inputs the model is uncertain about: the AU signal lives in the LLM’s behavior, not in the choice of e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot).

(2) Budget: gains saturate by (N,M)=(10,10)(N,M){=}(10,10). On TruthfulQA (Tab. 7(b)), TU AUROC climbs from 0.7550.755 at N=M=3N{=}M{=}3 to 0.8150.815 at (10,10)(10,10) under Cosine and then plateaus; the same saturation pattern holds on TriviaQA and under ROUGE-L (App. Tab. 18; full MM and NN sweeps with one dimension fixed in App. Tabs. 19, 19(b)). Headline runs use (N,M)=(20,20)(N,M){=}(20,20); validation experiments use (10,10)(10,10) (matched to SPUQ’s [13] KSPUQ=10K_{\mathrm{SPUQ}}{=}10). In practice, 3×33{\times}3 or 5×55{\times}5 suffices for screening and 10×1010{\times}10 yields stable components; adaptive stopping further cuts the median cost to 2525 generations with ≤0.014\leq 0.014 AUROC loss on TriviaQA (App. F.1.2).

(3) Perturbation, aggregation, and pool size are secondary. Noise scale ε\varepsilon has a validity–diversity sweet spot at ε=0.1\varepsilon{=}0.1 (AU AUROC peaks at ε\varepsilon∈[0.05,0.2]{\in}[0.05,0.2] on TruthfulQA, drops sharply at ε\varepsilon≥0.5{\geq}0.5; App. Tab. 23); perturbation mechanism is robust (paraphrase, distractor injection, instruction variation (strongest), and SPUQ-style noise all give non-trivial AU/EU under the two-level pipeline; App. Tab. 24); vector-to-scalar reduction (mean, sum, max, norm) shifts AU/TU AUROC by at most 0.050.05 (App. Tab. 26); paraphrase pool size shows a coverage–purity trade-off where Kpool∈[20,100]K_{\mathrm{pool}}{\in}[20,100] is also competitive (App. Tab. 30).

Default setting. A compute-efficient default derived from these ablations is (N,M)=(10,10)(N,M){=}(10,10), ε=0.1\varepsilon{=}0.1, Sentence-BERT, Kpool≈50K_{\mathrm{pool}}{\approx}50; pushing budget or pool size beyond this yields ≤0.02\leq 0.02 AUROC gain. Qualitative case studies of ambiguity- and knowledge-driven uncertainty regimes, including failure cases, are in App. G.

6 Conclusion

We introduced an inference-time, black-box UQ framework for LLMs that requires neither retraining nor access to token logits. By combining stochastic decoding within a fixed prompt with meaning-preserving perturbations across prompts, the framework applies the law of total covariance in embedding space to decompose predictive variability into within-perturbation (aleatoric, AU) and between-perturbation (epistemic, EU) components.

Theoretically, we establish a finite-MM bias identity with a closed-form correction, a Bayesian bridge whose conditions we measure as data-estimable diagnostics rather than assert, and a separation result identifying failures consistency-only UQ provably misses.

Empirically, the estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines across five benchmarks and four LLMs (Tab. 1), and under a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU (Tab. 2). Paired interventions demonstrate that AU and EU respond selectively to prompt ambiguity and knowledge gaps, capturing a disambiguation effect that fixed-prompt baselines miss (Tabs. 3, 5). Finite-MM bias validation, the claim-level long-form pilot, and comprehensive ablations further confirm the robustness of the decomposition (Tabs. 5–7).

Looking ahead, the AU/EU split can guide active data acquisition for high-EU queries [28, 39], selective retrieval in RAG [20, 50], adaptive sampling or tool invocation [48, 47], and conformal prediction in the black-box regime [40].

Limitations. (L1) Our estimators target perturbation-population AU/EU at fixed model weights, whose correspondence to Bayesian parameter uncertainty relies on the local regularity conditions diagnosed by D1–D3 (Sec. 4.2). (L2) Automated paraphrasing can introduce semantic drift that inflates between-prompt variance (App. F.2.3). (L3) Uncertainty estimates inherit the representational geometry and potential blind spots of the sentence encoder e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) (Tab. 7(a)). (L4) Nested sampling requires N​MNM decodes per query to separate AU and EU, incurring higher inference cost than single-level baselines (Sec. 5.3). (L5) Our empirical and interventional evaluations focus primarily on short-form QA with controlled single-factor interventions. See App. I for a detailed discussion.

Appendix A Additional Theoretical Details

Notation. We adopt the notation of Sec. 3: Z=e⁡(Y)∈ℝdZ=e(Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the embedded output, μ⁡(Δ)=𝔼⁡[Z∣Δ]\mu(\Delta)=\mathbb{E}[Z\!\mid\!\Delta] and Σ⁡(Δ)=Cov⁡(Z∣Δ)\Sigma(\Delta)=\mathrm{Cov}(Z\!\mid\!\Delta) the conditional moments, and (UA,UE,UT)(U_{A},U_{E},U_{T}) the population AU/EU/TU defined in Eq. (1). Throughout we assume 𝔼​‖Z‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|Z\|^{2}<\infty. The identity UT=UA+UEU_{T}=U_{A}+U_{E} is the law of total covariance and is taken as given. Standard tools (matrix-valued LLN, Hoeffding’s inequality, entrywise-to-Frobenius conversion) are used without re-derivation.

Roadmap and connection to the main paper.

Each appendix subsection backs up a specific main-paper claim. The dependency graph is:
