How to read the proofs. Within each subsection we follow the same pattern: state the assumptions, give the formal claim, prove it, and close with a one-line “what this gives the main paper.” Steps inside proofs are explicitly named (“Step 1: μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} is unbiased…”) so the reader can match the algebra to its intended role.

A.1 Two-Level Estimation with Finite Inner Sampling

Purpose of this subsection. The main paper’s Pillar 1 claims that the naive sample-covariance estimator of EU inflates the true EU by 1M​UA\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A} and that subtracting 1M​U^A\tfrac{1}{M}\hat{U}_{A} removes this inflation. This subsection establishes both: (i) the exact bias identity (Prop. A.1) that motivates the corrected estimator U^E\hat{U}_{E}, and (ii) the almost-sure consistency of U^A,U^Eraw,U^E\hat{U}_{A},\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}},\hat{U}_{E} as N→∞N\to\infty even with MM fixed (Thm. A.2). Finite-sample rates are deferred to App. A.2.

Sampling assumptions. Δ1,…,ΔN∼i​i​dpΔ\Delta_{1},\ldots,\Delta_{N}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}p_{\Delta}; conditional on Δi\Delta_{i}, Zi,1,…,Zi,MZ_{i,1},\ldots,Z_{i,M} are i.i.d. with the same distribution as Z|Δ=ΔiZ\!\mid\!\Delta=\Delta_{i}; the inner draws are mutually independent across ii; and 𝔼​‖Z‖4<∞\mathbb{E}\|Z\|^{4}<\infty. We label these (A1)–(A4) below and use them directly in proofs.

Estimators. The two-level estimators μ^i,Σ^i,U^A,U^Eraw\hat{\mu}_{i},\hat{\Sigma}_{i},\hat{U}_{A},\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}} are defined as in Alg. 1, and the bias-corrected epistemic estimator is

U^E:=U^Eraw−1M​U^A.\hat{U}_{E}\;:=\;\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}-\tfrac{1}{M}\hat{U}_{A}. (6)

The next subsection establishes the finite-MM identity that motivates this correction.

A.1.1 Unbiasedness and finite-MM bias identity

What we will show. Each inner-sample mean μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} is unbiased for the conditional mean μ⁡(Δi)\mu(\Delta_{i}), and each inner-sample covariance Σ^i\hat{\Sigma}_{i} is unbiased for the conditional covariance Σ⁡(Δi)\Sigma(\Delta_{i}). However, the unconditional covariance of μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} inherits a 1M​Σ​(Δi)\tfrac{1}{M}\Sigma(\Delta_{i}) inflation from inner sampling, which propagates through the law of total covariance into a 1M​UA\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A} inflation of the population covariance of μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i}. This is exactly the leakage the main-paper Pillar 1 references; the corrected estimator (6) subtracts it.

Proposition A.1 (Unbiasedness of Σ^i\hat{\Sigma}_{i} and finite-MM covariance inflation).

Under (A2) and 𝔼​‖Z‖2<∞\mathbb{E}\|Z\|^{2}<\infty,

𝔼⁡[Σ^i∣Δi]=Σ⁡(Δi),Cov⁡(μ^i∣Δi)=1M​Σ​(Δi),𝔼⁡[μ^i∣Δi]=μ⁡(Δi).\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\Sigma(\Delta_{i}),\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i})=\frac{1}{M}\Sigma(\Delta_{i}),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\mu(\Delta_{i}). (7)

Consequently, under (A1)–(A3),

Cov⁡(μ^i)=UE+1M​UA.\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i})=U_{E}+\frac{1}{M}U_{A}. (8)
Proof.

Fix ii and condition on Δi\Delta_{i}.

Step 1: 𝔼⁡[μ^i∣Δi]=μ⁡(Δi)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\mu(\Delta_{i}). This is immediate from linearity of conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[μ^i∣Δi]=1M​∑j=1M𝔼⁡[Zi,j∣Δi]=μ⁡(Δi).\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}[Z_{i,j}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\mu(\Delta_{i}).

Step 2: Cov⁡(μ^i∣Δi)=Σ⁡(Δi)/M\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i})=\Sigma(\Delta_{i})/M. Using conditional i.i.d. and Cov⁡(a​X)=a2​Cov​(X)\mathrm{Cov}(aX)=a^{2}\mathrm{Cov}(X),

Cov⁡(μ^i∣Δi)=Cov⁡(1M​∑j=1MZi,j|Δi)=1M2​∑j=1MCov⁡(Zi,j∣Δi)=1M​Σ​(Δi).\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i})=\mathrm{Cov}\!\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}Z_{i,j}\,\Big|\,\Delta_{i}\right)=\frac{1}{M^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathrm{Cov}(Z_{i,j}\mid\Delta_{i})=\frac{1}{M}\Sigma(\Delta_{i}).

Step 3: 𝔼⁡[Σ^i∣Δi]=Σ⁡(Δi)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\Sigma(\Delta_{i}). This is the standard unbiasedness of the sample covariance. A direct derivation: let Z~i,j:=Zi,j−μ⁡(Δi)\tilde{Z}_{i,j}:=Z_{i,j}-\mu(\Delta_{i}) and Z~¯i:=1M​∑jZ~i,j=μ^i−μ⁡(Δi)\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j}\tilde{Z}_{i,j}=\hat{\mu}_{i}-\mu(\Delta_{i}). Then

∑j=1M(Zi,j−μ^i)​(Zi,j−μ^i)⊤=∑j=1M(Z~i,j−Z~¯i)​(Z~i,j−Z~¯i)⊤=∑j=1MZ~i,j​Z~i,j⊤−M​Z~¯i​Z~¯i⊤.\sum_{j=1}^{M}(Z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})(Z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})^{\top}=\sum_{j=1}^{M}(\tilde{Z}_{i,j}-\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i})(\tilde{Z}_{i,j}-\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i})^{\top}=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\tilde{Z}_{i,j}\tilde{Z}_{i,j}^{\top}-M\,\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\,\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}^{\top}.

Taking conditional expectation and using conditional i.i.d. with 𝔼⁡[Z~i,j∣Δi]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i,j}\mid\Delta_{i}]=0,

𝔼⁡[∑j=1MZ~i,j​Z~i,j⊤|Δi]=M​𝔼​[Z~i,1​Z~i,1⊤∣Δi]=M​Σ​(Δi),\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M}\tilde{Z}_{i,j}\tilde{Z}_{i,j}^{\top}\,\Big|\,\Delta_{i}\right]=M\,\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Z}_{i,1}\tilde{Z}_{i,1}^{\top}\mid\Delta_{i}]=M\,\Sigma(\Delta_{i}),

and

𝔼⁡[M​Z~¯i​Z~¯i⊤|Δi]=M​Cov​(Z~¯i∣Δi)=M⋅1M​Σ​(Δi)=Σ⁡(Δi).\mathbb{E}\!\left[M\,\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\,\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}^{\top}\,\Big|\,\Delta_{i}\right]=M\,\mathrm{Cov}(\overline{\tilde{Z}}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i})=M\cdot\frac{1}{M}\Sigma(\Delta_{i})=\Sigma(\Delta_{i}).

Therefore,

𝔼⁡[∑j=1M(Zi,j−μ^i)​(Zi,j−μ^i)⊤|Δi]=(M−1)​Σ​(Δi),\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M}(Z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})(Z_{i,j}-\hat{\mu}_{i})^{\top}\,\Big|\,\Delta_{i}\right]=(M-1)\Sigma(\Delta_{i}),

and dividing by (M−1)(M-1) gives 𝔼⁡[Σ^i∣Δi]=Σ⁡(Δi)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]=\Sigma(\Delta_{i}).

Step 4: unconditional covariance inflation. Apply the law of total covariance to μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} with conditioning variable Δi\Delta_{i}:

Cov⁡(μ^i)=𝔼⁡[Cov⁡(μ^i∣Δi)]+Cov⁡(𝔼⁡[μ^i∣Δi])=𝔼⁡[1M​Σ​(Δi)]+Cov⁡(μ⁡(Δi))=1M​UA+UE.\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i})=\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i})\big]+\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mu}_{i}\mid\Delta_{i}]\big)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{M}\Sigma(\Delta_{i})\Big]+\mathrm{Cov}(\mu(\Delta_{i}))=\frac{1}{M}U_{A}+U_{E}.

This yields (8). ∎

What this gives the main paper. The identity Cov⁡(μ^i)=UE+1M​UA\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{i})=U_{E}+\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A} is the inflation we corrected for in Eq. (6) and that the main-paper Prop. 4.1 reports informally. Because the inflation is exact (not asymptotic), the corrected estimator U^E\hat{U}_{E} has the right target at every M≥2M\geq 2, which is what enables AU/EU separation at the small inner budgets a black-box API forces.

A.1.2 Almost sure consistency (raw and corrected forms)

Theorem A.2 (Almost sure consistency of two-level estimators).

Under (A1)–(A4): (i) if M→∞M\to\infty and N→∞N\to\infty, then U^A→a.s.UA\hat{U}_{A}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{A} and U^Eraw→a.s.UE\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{E}; (ii) if N→∞N\to\infty while M≥2M\geq 2 is fixed, then U^A→a.s.UA\hat{U}_{A}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{A}, U^Eraw→a.s.UE+1M​UA\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{E}+\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A}, and U^E→a.s.UE\hat{U}_{E}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{E}.

Proof sketch.

U^A→a.s.UA\hat{U}_{A}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{A} is the matrix-valued SLLN applied to i.i.d. {Σ^i}\{\hat{\Sigma}_{i}\} with 𝔼⁡[Σ^1]=UA\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Sigma}_{1}]=U_{A} by Prop. A.1; U^Eraw→a.s.UE+1M​UA\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}U_{E}+\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A} is the sample-covariance SLLN on i.i.d. {μ^i}\{\hat{\mu}_{i}\}, with population value identified by Prop. A.1. Combining gives U^E=U^Eraw−1M​U^A→UE\hat{U}_{E}=\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}-\tfrac{1}{M}\hat{U}_{A}\to U_{E}, i.e. (ii); (i) follows by additionally letting M→∞M\to\infty. ∎

The corrected estimator U^E\hat{U}_{E} defined in Alg. 1 is therefore unbiased for UEU_{E} at any M≥2M\geq 2 and converges to it as N→∞N\!\to\!\infty. The rate is in App. A.2.

A.2 Finite-Sample Concentration and Two-Level Monte Carlo Bounds

Purpose of this subsection. App. A.1 established whether U^A,U^E\hat{U}_{A},\hat{U}_{E} converge to their population targets; this subsection establishes how fast. The result the main-paper Pillar 1 quotes informally (O⁡(log⁡(1/δ)/N)O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/N}) plus lower-order 1/M1/M terms) is Theorem A.5. We get there in two steps: first an outer-only bound that pretends conditional moments μ⁡(Δ),Σ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta),\Sigma(\Delta) are known exactly (Thm. A.3), then the full two-level bound that adds the inner-sampling fluctuation back in.

The proofs combine standard tools (Hoeffding’s inequality for bounded centered i.i.d. scalars and the entrywise-to-Frobenius conversion ‖A‖F≤d​‖A‖max\|A\|_{F}\leq d\|A\|_{\max} for A∈ℝd×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}) with the two-level sampling decomposition specific to our estimator. We refer to either as “standard” below.

A.2.1 Outer concentration with population conditional moments

As a stepping stone to the full two-level bound, we first treat μ⁡(Δ),Σ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta),\Sigma(\Delta) as known (infinite inner samples). Let μi:=μ⁡(Δi)\mu_{i}\!:=\!\mu(\Delta_{i}), Σi:=Σ⁡(Δi)\Sigma_{i}\!:=\!\Sigma(\Delta_{i}), U^A:=1N​∑iΣi\widehat{U}_{A}\!:=\!\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\Sigma_{i}, U^E:=1N−1​∑i(μi−μ¯⋆)​(μi−μ¯⋆)⊤\widehat{U}_{E}\!:=\!\tfrac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i}(\mu_{i}-\bar{\mu}^{\star})(\mu_{i}-\bar{\mu}^{\star})^{\top} with μ¯⋆:=1N​∑iμi\bar{\mu}^{\star}\!:=\!\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}.

Theorem A.3 (High-probability outer concentration).

Assume Δ1,…,ΔN\Delta_{1},\ldots,\Delta_{N} i.i.d. with ‖Σ⁡(Δ)‖F≤BΣ\|\Sigma(\Delta)\|_{F}\!\leq\!B_{\Sigma} and ‖μ⁡(Δ)‖2≤Bμ\|\mu(\Delta)\|_{2}\!\leq\!B_{\mu} a.s. For any δ∈(0,1)\delta\!\in\!(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

‖U^A−UA‖F\displaystyle\|\widehat{U}_{A}-U_{A}\|_{F} ≤d​BΣ​2​log⁡(2​d2/δ)/N,\displaystyle\leq d\,B_{\Sigma}\sqrt{2\log(2d^{2}/\delta)/N}, (9)
‖U^E−UE‖F\displaystyle\|\widehat{U}_{E}-U_{E}\|_{F} ≤NN−1​[d​Bμ2​2​log⁡(2​d2/δ)/N+2​d​Bμ2​2​log⁡(2​d/δ)/N].\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{N}{N-1}\!\left[d\,B_{\mu}^{2}\sqrt{2\log(2d^{2}/\delta)/N}+2d\,B_{\mu}^{2}\sqrt{2\log(2d/\delta)/N}\right]. (10)
Proof sketch.

For (9): entrywise Hoeffding on the centered, bounded scalars (Σi)k​ℓ−(UA)k​ℓ(\Sigma_{i})_{k\ell}-(U_{A})_{k\ell} (b=2​BΣb\!=\!2B_{\Sigma}), union bound over d2d^{2} entries, and the entrywise-to-Frobenius conversion ‖A‖F≤d​‖A‖max\|A\|_{F}\leq d\|A\|_{\max}. For (10): write U^E−UE=NN−1​[(Q¯−Q)−(M¯−m​m⊤)]\widehat{U}_{E}-U_{E}=\tfrac{N}{N-1}[(\bar{Q}\!-\!Q)-(\bar{M}\!-\!mm^{\top})] with Q=𝔼⁡[μ​μ⊤]Q\!=\!\mathbb{E}[\mu\mu^{\top}], m=𝔼⁡[μ]m\!=\!\mathbb{E}[\mu], and the sample analogues. Apply (i) entrywise Hoeffding+union to Q¯−Q\bar{Q}\!-\!Q, (ii) coordinatewise Hoeffding+union to μ¯⋆−m\bar{\mu}^{\star}\!-\!m, and (iii) the identity M¯−m​m⊤=μ¯⋆​(μ¯⋆−m)⊤+(μ¯⋆−m)​m⊤\bar{M}-mm^{\top}=\bar{\mu}^{\star}(\bar{\mu}^{\star}-m)^{\top}+(\bar{\mu}^{\star}-m)m^{\top} with ‖μ¯⋆‖2,‖m‖2≤Bμ\|\bar{\mu}^{\star}\|_{2},\|m\|_{2}\!\leq\!B_{\mu} to get ‖M¯−m​m⊤‖F≤2​Bμ​‖μ¯⋆−m‖2\|\bar{M}-mm^{\top}\|_{F}\leq 2B_{\mu}\|\bar{\mu}^{\star}-m\|_{2}. Triangle inequality and constant-simplification on the intersection event give (10). ∎

The leading log⁡(1/δ)/N\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/N} rate matches what main-paper Pillar 1 quotes; dd is the embedding dimension, entering both as a linear prefactor dd and logarithmically inside log⁡(2​d2/δ)/N\sqrt{\log(2d^{2}/\delta)/N}.

A.2.2 Two-level Monte Carlo concentration (outer NN, inner MM)

Why this step. The previous subsubsection assumed exact conditional moments, which we never have in practice; we estimate them from MM inner draws. This subsection adds the inner-sampling slack and gives the rate the main paper actually relies on, with both NN and MM explicit.

To obtain explicit finite-sample bounds, we impose an a.s. boundedness assumption on embedded outputs.

Assumption A.4 (Bounded embedded outputs).

Almost surely, ‖Z‖2≤BZ\|Z\|_{2}\leq B_{Z}. Equivalently, for all (i,j)(i,j), ‖Zi,j‖2≤BZ\|Z_{i,j}\|_{2}\leq B_{Z} a.s.

Under Assumption A.4, we have ‖μ⁡(Δ)‖2≤BZ\|\mu(\Delta)\|_{2}\leq B_{Z} and ‖Σ⁡(Δ)‖F≤2​BZ2\|\Sigma(\Delta)\|_{F}\leq 2B_{Z}^{2} a.s. (the latter follows from ‖Z−μ‖2≤2​BZ\|Z-\mu\|_{2}\leq 2B_{Z} and ‖v​v⊤‖F=‖v‖22\|vv^{\top}\|_{F}=\|v\|_{2}^{2}).

Plan. We bound (i) ‖U^A−UA‖F\|\hat{U}_{A}-U_{A}\|_{F} and (ii) ‖U^E−UE‖F\|\hat{U}_{E}-U_{E}\|_{F} with explicit dependence on NN and MM. The key is to decompose each estimator into an outer fluctuation term (from sampling Δi\Delta_{i}) plus an inner fluctuation term (from estimating μ⁡(Δi),Σ⁡(Δi)\mu(\Delta_{i}),\Sigma(\Delta_{i}) with MM samples).

Inner-sample concentration (used below). For any fixed ii and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), conditional on Δi\Delta_{i}, standard Hoeffding gives ‖μ^i−μ⁡(Δi)‖2≤2​BZ​2​d​log⁡(2​d/δ)/M\|\hat{\mu}_{i}-\mu(\Delta_{i})\|_{2}\leq 2B_{Z}\sqrt{2d\log(2d/\delta)/M} w.p. ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta (coordinate-wise + ‖v‖2≤d​‖v‖∞\|v\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\|v\|_{\infty}), and ‖Σ^i−Σ⁡(Δi)‖F≤C​BZ2​d​log⁡(2​d2/δ)/M\|\hat{\Sigma}_{i}-\Sigma(\Delta_{i})\|_{F}\leq C\,B_{Z}^{2}\,d\,\sqrt{\log(2d^{2}/\delta)/M} w.p. ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta for a universal C>0C>0 (entrywise Hoeffding on 1M​∑jZi,j​Zi,j⊤\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{j}Z_{i,j}Z_{i,j}^{\top} plus the rank-1 perturbation μ^i​μ^i⊤−μi​μi⊤\hat{\mu}_{i}\hat{\mu}_{i}^{\top}-\mu_{i}\mu_{i}^{\top} controlled by the mean bound).

Theorem A.5 (Two-level Monte Carlo concentration (explicit N,MN,M rates)).

Assume (A1)–(A3) and Assumption A.4. Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

‖U^A−UA‖F\displaystyle\|\hat{U}_{A}-U_{A}\|_{F} ≤d⁡(2​BZ2)​2​log⁡(4​d2/δ)N+C1​BZ2​d​log⁡(4​d2/δ)M+C1​BZ2​d​log⁡(4​d2/δ)N​M,\displaystyle\leq d\,(2B_{Z}^{2})\sqrt{\frac{2\log(4d^{2}/\delta)}{N}}\;+\;C_{1}\,B_{Z}^{2}\,d\,\sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^{2}/\delta)}{M}}\;+\;C_{1}\,B_{Z}^{2}\,d\,\sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^{2}/\delta)}{NM}}, (11)
‖U^E−UE‖F\displaystyle\|\hat{U}_{E}-U_{E}\|_{F} ≤C2​BZ2​d​log⁡(4​d2/δ)N+C3​BZ2​d​log⁡(4​d2/δ)N​M+1M​‖U^A−UA‖F,\displaystyle\leq C_{2}\,B_{Z}^{2}\,d\,\sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^{2}/\delta)}{N}}\;+\;C_{3}\,B_{Z}^{2}\,d\,\sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^{2}/\delta)}{NM}}\;+\;\frac{1}{M}\,\|\hat{U}_{A}-U_{A}\|_{F}, (12)

for universal constants C1,C2,C3>0C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}>0.

Proof sketch.

Decompose U^A−UA=(1N​∑iΣ⁡(Δi)−UA)+1N​∑i(Σ^i−Σ⁡(Δi))\hat{U}_{A}-U_{A}=(\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\Sigma(\Delta_{i})-U_{A})+\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}(\hat{\Sigma}_{i}-\Sigma(\Delta_{i})). The first term is bounded by Thm. A.3 with BΣ≤2​BZ2B_{\Sigma}\leq 2B_{Z}^{2}, giving the log/N\sqrt{\log/N} term; the per-ii inner Hoeffding above and a union bound over ii give the log/M\sqrt{\log/M} term; exploiting cross-outer independence (A3) when union-bounding entrywise yields the sharper log/(N​M)\sqrt{\log/(NM)} refinement. For U^E\hat{U}_{E}, write U^E−UE=(U^Eraw−(UE+1M​UA))+1M​(UA−U^A)\hat{U}_{E}-U_{E}=(\hat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}-(U_{E}+\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A}))+\tfrac{1}{M}(U_{A}-\hat{U}_{A}); the first piece is the sample-covariance error of {μ^i}\{\hat{\mu}_{i}\} around their population covariance UE+1M​UAU_{E}+\tfrac{1}{M}U_{A} (Prop. A.1) and is bounded by Thm. A.3 with ‖μ^‖2≤BZ\|\hat{\mu}\|_{2}\leq B_{Z}, while the second is 1/M1/M times the bound from U^A\hat{U}_{A}. ∎

Remark. Assumption A.4 can be relaxed to sub-Gaussian or bounded-moment conditions by replacing Hoeffding by Bernstein; the (N,M)(N,M) rates are unchanged.

What this gives the main paper. Pillar 1 in Sec. 4.1 states informally that the bias-corrected estimator concentrates at O⁡(log⁡(1/δ)/N)O(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/N}) plus lower-order 1/M1/M terms. (11)–(12) are the precise version. The 1/(N​M)1/(NM) refinement matters in practice: it tells us that doubling the inner budget MM buys us a comparable rate improvement to doubling the outer budget NN, which is what justifies the equal-budget default N=M≈10N{=}M{\approx}10 in the experiments.

A.3 Explicit Sufficient Conditions for the Bayesian Bridge

Purpose of this subsection. The main paper’s Pillar 2 (Thm. 4.2) states that the perturbation-population uncertainties (UAΔ,UEΔ)(U_{A}^{\Delta},U_{E}^{\Delta}) approximate the Bayesian targets (UABayes,UEBayes)(U_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}},U_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}) up to two defect terms εA,εE\varepsilon_{A},\varepsilon_{E}. Here we make these defects explicit by introducing local conditions on the model and bounding εA,εE\varepsilon_{A},\varepsilon_{E} in those terms.

Structure of this subsection. We treat the EU- and AU-side bridges separately. The EU bridge (§A.3.2) needs (i) local linearity of the conditional mean in both parameters and inputs (Ass. A.6), (ii) a local Gaussian posterior (Ass. A.7), and (iii) a semantic coverage condition saying the perturbation distribution spans the directions of Bayesian mean variation (Ass. A.8). The AU bridge (§A.3.3) needs only one extra piece (a Lipschitz aleatoric map; Ass. A.11) saying decoding stochasticity varies smoothly with the predictive state. Each assumption gets a Discussion block addressing its plausibility and how to measure its tightness from data (see also App. C for the diagnostics).

Relation to Wang and Ji [53]. Our outer ensemble builds on the local input–parameter correspondence of Wang and Ji [53], while our bridge theorems below quantify its approximation error at the distributional level. Specifically, Prop. 3.3 of Wang and Ji [53] is a pointwise, first-order existence result in a continuous input space: for a small parameter shift δ​θ\delta\theta, there exists a (generally non-unique) continuous input perturbation δ​x\delta x inducing the same first-order output change, and vice versa via a first-layer construction. However, pointwise existence neither provides a mechanism for generating meaning-preserving perturbations of discrete text nor guarantees that the chosen input-perturbation distribution matches the pushforward of the parameter posterior—a prerequisite for covariance-level AU/EU approximation. Our two-stage procedure (Sec. 3) instantiates a localized perturbation distribution over a finite pool of fluent paraphrases: isotropic Gaussian noise in embedding space serves purely as a stochastic selector over cached candidates, ensuring the LLM only processes natural text. The remaining approximation gaps are explicitly tracked by our diagnostics: D1 for local linearization, D3 for distributional coverage, and our validity audit (App. F.2.3) for semantic preservation. Beyond Wang and Ji [53], our technical contributions encompass the nested two-level estimator, the exact finite-MM bias identity and correction, and the conditional AU/EU bridge bounds with data-estimable defect diagnostics.

A.3.1 Notation recap and three formally distinct flavors of (UA,UE,UT)(U_{A},U_{E},U_{T})

Fix an input xx and trained parameters θ⋆\theta^{\star}. Let Δ∼pΔ\Delta\sim p_{\Delta} be a semantic perturbation and xΔ:=T⁡(x,Δ)x_{\Delta}:=T(x,\Delta). For the stochastic model output representation Zθ​(x,ξ)Z_{\theta}(x,\xi) (decoding noise ξ\xi; embedding Z=e⁡(Y)Z=e(Y), main paper), define the conditional mean and covariance

mθ(x):=𝔼ξ[Zθ(x,ξ)∣x,θ],Σθ(x):=Covξ(Zθ(x,ξ)∣x,θ).m_{\theta}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[Z_{\theta}(x,\xi)\mid x,\theta],\qquad\Sigma_{\theta}(x):=\mathrm{Cov}_{\xi}(Z_{\theta}(x,\xi)\mid x,\theta).

The paper uses three formally distinct flavors of (UA,UE,UT)(U_{A},U_{E},U_{T}) that are easy to conflate; we lay them out once here for reference, and the two pillars (Sec. 4.1 and 4.2) bound the gaps between them.

(1) Bayesian (ground-truth) AU/EU/TU.

Defined over the parameter posterior p⁡(θ∣𝒟)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D}) as in the canonical Bayesian decomposition [23, 8]:

𝒰ABayes​(x):=𝔼θ∼p⁡(θ∣𝒟)​[Σθ​(x)],𝒰EBayes​(x):=Covθ∼p⁡(θ∣𝒟)​(mθ​(x)),𝒰TBayes​(x):=𝒰ABayes​(x)+𝒰EBayes​(x).\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})}\!\big[\Sigma_{\theta}(x)\big],\quad\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x):=\mathrm{Cov}_{\theta\sim p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D})}\!\big(m_{\theta}(x)\big),\quad\mathcal{U}_{T}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x):=\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)+\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x). (13)

This is the object Bayesian UQ ultimately seeks. We never sample from p⁡(θ∣𝒟)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D}) directly: the posterior over an LLM’s parameters is intractable.

(2) Perturbation-population AU/EU/TU (what our estimator targets).

At the fixed deployed model θ⋆\theta^{\star}, replace the parameter average by an outer-perturbation average over pΔp_{\Delta}:

𝒰AΔ​(x):=𝔼Δ∼pΔ​[Σθ⋆​(xΔ)],𝒰EΔ​(x):=CovΔ∼pΔ​(mθ⋆​(xΔ)),𝒰TΔ​(x):=𝒰AΔ​(x)+𝒰EΔ​(x).\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{\Delta\sim p_{\Delta}}\!\big[\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\big],\quad\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}(x):=\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta\sim p_{\Delta}}\!\big(m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\big),\quad\mathcal{U}_{T}^{\Delta}(x):=\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x)+\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}(x). (14)

By the law of total covariance applied to the joint distribution of (Δ,ξ)(\Delta,\xi) at θ=θ⋆\theta=\theta^{\star}, the 𝒰TΔ​(x)\mathcal{U}_{T}^{\Delta}(x) defined above coincides with the embedding-space total covariance Cov​(Z)=UT​(x)\mathrm{Cov}(Z)=U_{T}(x) written in Eq. (1) of the main paper, so (UA,UE,UT)≡(𝒰AΔ,𝒰EΔ,𝒰TΔ)(U_{A},U_{E},U_{T})\equiv(\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta},\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta},\mathcal{U}_{T}^{\Delta}) in that equation. These quantities are well-defined for any LLM with black-box sampling access; sampling from pΔp_{\Delta} replaces sampling from the parameter posterior.

(3) Empirical estimators (what we actually compute at run time).

The two-level Monte Carlo estimators built from NN outer perturbations {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and MM inner decodes {Zi,j}j=1M\{Z_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{M} per perturbation:

U^A(M):=1N​∑i=1NΣ^i,U^Eraw:=Cov^​({μ^i}i=1N),U^E(M):=U^Eraw−1M​U^A(M),\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)}:=\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widehat{\Sigma}_{i},\quad\widehat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}:=\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\!\big(\{\hat{\mu}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\big),\quad\widehat{U}_{E}^{(M)}:=\widehat{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{raw}}-\tfrac{1}{M}\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)}, (15)

where μ^i\hat{\mu}_{i} and Σ^i\widehat{\Sigma}_{i} are the sample mean and sample covariance of {Zi,j}j=1M\{Z_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{M}. The bias-corrected U^E(M)\widehat{U}_{E}^{(M)} is the estimator we use throughout the paper; we drop the (M)(M) superscript when there is no ambiguity.

How the three flavors relate.

Pillar 1 (App. A.1 and A.2) bounds the gap (3)→(2)(3)\!\to\!(2): U^A(M)→𝒰AΔ\widehat{U}_{A}^{(M)}\to\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta} and U^E(M)→𝒰EΔ\widehat{U}_{E}^{(M)}\to\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta} almost surely as N→∞N\to\infty at any fixed M≥2M\geq 2, with the 1M\tfrac{1}{M} leakage from inner-sampling fluctuation removed by the bias correction. Pillar 2 (this subsection) bounds the gap (2)→(1)(2)\!\to\!(1): under three local conditions on the model around xx, ‖𝒰∙Δ​(x)−𝒰∙Bayes​(x)‖F\|\mathcal{U}_{\bullet}^{\Delta}(x)-\mathcal{U}_{\bullet}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)\|_{F} is upper-bounded by defect terms εA​(x),εE​(x)\varepsilon_{A}(x),\varepsilon_{E}(x) that we estimate empirically as diagnostics from the outputs the estimator already collects (App. C). The composition of the two pillars yields the end-to-end bound ‖U^∙(M)−𝒰∙Bayes‖F≤MC error+bridge defect\|\widehat{U}_{\bullet}^{(M)}-\mathcal{U}_{\bullet}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}\|_{F}\leq\text{MC error}+\text{bridge defect} stated informally in Theorem 4.2 of the main paper.

A.3.2 Epistemic bridge via linearization and semantic coverage

Assumption A.6 (Local bi-linearization of the conditional mean).

There exist Jacobians Jθ​(x)∈ℝd×PJ_{\theta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P} and Jx​(x)∈ℝd×qJ_{x}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} and constants cθ,cx>0c_{\theta},c_{x}>0 such that for small δ​θ\delta\theta and δ​x\delta x,

mθ⋆+δ​θ​(x)\displaystyle m_{\theta^{\star}+\delta\theta}(x) =mθ⋆​(x)+Jθ​(x)​δ​θ+rθ,‖rθ‖≤cθ​‖δ​θ‖2,\displaystyle=m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{\theta}(x)\,\delta\theta+r_{\theta},\qquad\|r_{\theta}\|\leq c_{\theta}\|\delta\theta\|^{2}, (16)
mθ⋆​(x+δ​x)\displaystyle m_{\theta^{\star}}(x+\delta x) =mθ⋆​(x)+Jx​(x)​δ​x+rx,‖rx‖≤cx​‖δ​x‖2.\displaystyle=m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{x}(x)\,\delta x+r_{x},\qquad\|r_{x}\|\leq c_{x}\|\delta x\|^{2}. (17)
Assumption A.7 (Local Gaussian posterior approximation).

In a neighborhood of θ⋆\theta^{\star}, the Bayesian posterior admits a local approximation δ​θ:=θ−θ⋆∼𝒩⁡(0,Σθ)\delta\theta:=\theta-\theta^{\star}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\theta}).

Discussion of Assumptions A.6–A.7.

Two readings of these assumptions deserve direct engagement: that NTK-style linearization fits modern LLMs poorly at the global level, and that RLHF/DPO breaks classical Bayesian-posterior assumptions. Both turn on the distinction between global and local regimes, which we now make explicit.

(i) Linearization is local, not global. Assumption A.6 only requires a local first-order Taylor expansion of mθ​(x)m_{\theta}(x) around the fixed reference (θ⋆,x)(\theta^{\star},x), with second-order remainder ‖r‖≤c​‖δ‖2\|r\|\leq c\|\delta\|^{2}. This is strictly weaker than the global NTK regime that underlies infinite-width arguments for full networks [55]. Local first-order linearization for language models has been studied directly [51], where it provides a useful regime for analyzing fine-tuning trajectories. In our usage we need linearity only inside the moderate-ε\varepsilon semantic neighborhood the perturbation distribution actually populates, and the residual is empirically measurable via the OLS diagnostic D1 in App. C.

(ii) Locally Gaussian posterior is the Laplace assumption. Assumption A.7 is the standard Laplace approximation to the posterior in a neighborhood of a twice-differentiable local minimum, applied around θ⋆\theta^{\star}. Recent work has applied this exact approximation to large language models in the Bayesian-LoRA line [60], where it gives competitive posterior surrogates for instruction-tuned LLMs. The training procedure (RLHF, DPO, or standard MLE) only determines which local minimum θ⋆\theta^{\star} sits at, not whether the posterior shape near θ⋆\theta^{\star} is locally Gaussian; any twice-differentiable loss admits a local quadratic and hence a local Gaussian posterior. Our diagnostic D2 (Henze–Zirkler test on embedding samples; specifically the inner-decode and outer-mean clouds in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, not on uncertainty scores; App. C) flags inputs where the embedding distribution induced by Assumption A.7 (under the linearity in Assumption A.6) visibly fails to be Gaussian.

(iii) Coverage and stability are measurable. Assumptions A.8 and A.11 are not assertions of fact but defect terms that appear in our bounds: the bridge gets tighter as εcov→0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}\to 0 and as the aleatoric Lipschitz constant decreases. Both are upper-bounded by computable quantities (D3 MMD upper bound; spread of Σ^i\hat{\Sigma}_{i} across ii). The bounds remain meaningful with non-zero defects; they quantify, rather than presuppose, how well the perturbation mechanism approximates Bayesian posterior sampling.

(iv) Existing UQ methods make analogous local assumptions. MC-Dropout assumes the dropout-induced distribution approximates a Bayesian posterior locally; Deep Ensembles assume independently trained models sample meaningfully from the posterior; Laplace approximations assume local Gaussianity. Our assumptions are at the same level of mathematical commitment, with the additional property that we measure their tightness on each dataset rather than asserting them globally.

Define the Bayesian mean-variation operator

A⁡(x):=Jθ​(x)​Σθ1/2∈ℝd×P.A(x):=J_{\theta}(x)\,\Sigma_{\theta}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times P}. (18)

Under Assumptions A.6–A.7, the linearized Bayesian epistemic covariance of the mean is

𝒰EBayes​(x)=Covθ​(mθ​(x))=A⁡(x)​A​(x)⊤+Remθ,\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)=\mathrm{Cov}_{\theta}(m_{\theta}(x))=A(x)A(x)^{\top}+\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}, (19)

where Remθ\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta} aggregates second-order terms.

Assumption A.8 (Semantic coverage defect).

Let PxP_{x} be the orthogonal projector onto Im​(Jx​(x))\mathrm{Im}(J_{x}(x)). Define the semantic coverage defect

εcov​(x):=‖(I−Px)​A​(x)‖F.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x):=\|(I-P_{x})A(x)\|_{F}. (20)
Lemma A.9 (Best-match perturbation covariance for epistemic variation).

There exists ΣΔ⋆⪰0\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}\succeq 0 such that

‖Jx​(x)​ΣΔ⋆​Jx​(x)⊤−A⁡(x)​A​(x)⊤‖F≤ 2​‖A⁡(x)‖F​εcov​(x)+εcov​(x)2.\left\|J_{x}(x)\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}(x)^{\top}-A(x)A(x)^{\top}\right\|_{F}\;\leq\;2\|A(x)\|_{F}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)^{2}. (21)

If εcov​(x)=0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)=0, equality holds.

Proof.

Let PxP_{x} be the projector onto Im⁡(Jx)\mathrm{Im}(J_{x}) and decompose A=A∥+A⟂A=A_{\parallel}+A_{\perp} with A∥:=Px​AA_{\parallel}:=P_{x}A and A⟂:=(I−Px)​AA_{\perp}:=(I-P_{x})A. Since A∥∈Im⁡(Jx)A_{\parallel}\in\mathrm{Im}(J_{x}), there exists BB such that A∥=Jx​BA_{\parallel}=J_{x}B. Set ΣΔ⋆:=B​B⊤⪰0\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}:=BB^{\top}\succeq 0, giving Jx​ΣΔ⋆​Jx⊤=A∥​A∥⊤J_{x}\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}^{\top}=A_{\parallel}A_{\parallel}^{\top}. Now expand

A​A⊤−A∥​A∥⊤=A⟂​A⟂⊤+A∥​A⟂⊤+A⟂​A∥⊤,AA^{\top}-A_{\parallel}A_{\parallel}^{\top}=A_{\perp}A_{\perp}^{\top}+A_{\parallel}A_{\perp}^{\top}+A_{\perp}A_{\parallel}^{\top},

and bound Frobenius norms using ‖A⟂‖F=εcov​(x)\|A_{\perp}\|_{F}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x):

‖A​A⊤−A∥​A∥⊤‖F≤‖A⟂​A⟂⊤‖F+‖A∥​A⟂⊤‖F+‖A⟂​A∥⊤‖F≤‖A⟂‖F2+2​‖A∥‖F​‖A⟂‖F≤εcov​(x)2+2​‖A‖F​εcov​(x).\|AA^{\top}-A_{\parallel}A_{\parallel}^{\top}\|_{F}\leq\|A_{\perp}A_{\perp}^{\top}\|_{F}+\|A_{\parallel}A_{\perp}^{\top}\|_{F}+\|A_{\perp}A_{\parallel}^{\top}\|_{F}\leq\|A_{\perp}\|_{F}^{2}+2\|A_{\parallel}\|_{F}\|A_{\perp}\|_{F}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)^{2}+2\|A\|_{F}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x).

This proves (21). ∎

Theorem A.10 (Epistemic bridge bound).

Under Assumptions A.6–A.8, the perturbation-population epistemic covariance satisfies

‖𝒰EΔ​(x)−𝒰EBayes​(x)‖F≤2​‖A⁡(x)‖F​εcov​(x)+εcov​(x)2⏟coverage+Cθ​𝔼​‖rθ‖+Cx​𝔼​‖rx‖+‖Remθ‖F⏟linearization remainders,\|\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}(x)-\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)\|_{F}\;\leq\;\underbrace{2\|A(x)\|_{F}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)^{2}}_{\textnormal{coverage}}+\underbrace{C_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}\|r_{\theta}\|+C_{x}\,\mathbb{E}\|r_{x}\|+\|\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}\|_{F}}_{\textnormal{linearization remainders}}, (22)

where expectations are taken over δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,Σθ)\delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\theta}) and δ​x:=xΔ−x\delta x:=x_{\Delta}-x, and Cθ,CxC_{\theta},C_{x} are absolute constants (depending only on the chosen norms).

Proof.

We provide a detailed proof with explicit decompositions.

Step 1: Bayesian epistemic covariance under local linearization. Under (16),

mθ⋆+δ​θ​(x)=mθ⋆​(x)+Jθ​(x)​δ​θ+rθ.m_{\theta^{\star}+\delta\theta}(x)=m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{\theta}(x)\delta\theta+r_{\theta}.

Taking covariance over δ​θ\delta\theta,

Covθ​(mθ​(x))=Cov⁡(Jθ​δ​θ+rθ)=Jθ​Cov​(δ​θ)​Jθ⊤+Cov⁡(rθ)+Cov⁡(Jθ​δ​θ,rθ)+Cov⁡(rθ,Jθ​δ​θ).\mathrm{Cov}_{\theta}(m_{\theta}(x))=\mathrm{Cov}\big(J_{\theta}\delta\theta+r_{\theta}\big)=J_{\theta}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\delta\theta)\,J_{\theta}^{\top}+\mathrm{Cov}(r_{\theta})+\mathrm{Cov}(J_{\theta}\delta\theta,r_{\theta})+\mathrm{Cov}(r_{\theta},J_{\theta}\delta\theta).

Under Assumption A.7, Cov⁡(δ​θ)=Σθ\mathrm{Cov}(\delta\theta)=\Sigma_{\theta} and thus the leading term is Jθ​Σθ​Jθ⊤=A⁡(x)​A​(x)⊤J_{\theta}\Sigma_{\theta}J_{\theta}^{\top}=A(x)A(x)^{\top} by definition of A⁡(x)A(x). Collect the remaining terms into Remθ\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}:

𝒰EBayes​(x)=A⁡(x)​A​(x)⊤+Remθ.\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)=A(x)A(x)^{\top}+\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}.

A standard norm bound yields ‖Remθ‖F≤Cθ​𝔼​‖rθ‖+(higher-order terms)\|\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}\|_{F}\leq C_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}\|r_{\theta}\|+\text{(higher-order terms)}, which is the term displayed in (22).

Step 2: Perturbation-population epistemic covariance under input linearization. Under (17),

mθ⋆​(xΔ)=mθ⋆​(x+δ​x)=mθ⋆​(x)+Jx​(x)​δ​x+rx.m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})=m_{\theta^{\star}}(x+\delta x)=m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{x}(x)\delta x+r_{x}.

Taking covariance over Δ\Delta (equivalently over δ​x\delta x),

𝒰EΔ​(x)=CovΔ​(mθ⋆​(xΔ))=CovΔ​(Jx​δ​x+rx)=Jx​Cov​(δ​x)​Jx⊤+Remx,\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}(x)=\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta}\big(m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\big)=\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta}\big(J_{x}\delta x+r_{x}\big)=J_{x}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\delta x)\,J_{x}^{\top}+\mathrm{Rem}_{x},

where Remx\mathrm{Rem}_{x} collects Cov⁡(rx)\mathrm{Cov}(r_{x}) and cross-covariance terms between Jx​δ​xJ_{x}\delta x and rxr_{x}. Using triangle inequality and standard covariance bounds, one obtains ‖Remx‖F≤Cx​𝔼​‖rx‖\|\mathrm{Rem}_{x}\|_{F}\leq C_{x}\,\mathbb{E}\|r_{x}\| for an absolute constant CxC_{x}.

Step 3: Coverage approximation. Lemma A.9 provides ΣΔ⋆⪰0\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}\succeq 0 such that

‖Jx​ΣΔ⋆​Jx⊤−A​A⊤‖F≤2​‖A‖F​εcov+εcov2.\|J_{x}\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}^{\top}-AA^{\top}\|_{F}\leq 2\|A\|_{F}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}^{2}.

Interpret ΣΔ⋆\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star} as the “best-match” covariance in input-perturbation space that aligns perturbation-induced mean variation with Bayesian mean-variation directions (up to the defect).

Step 4: Combine all terms. Combine the decompositions:

𝒰EΔ=Jx​Cov​(δ​x)​Jx⊤+Remx,𝒰EBayes=A​A⊤+Remθ.\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}=J_{x}\mathrm{Cov}(\delta x)J_{x}^{\top}+\mathrm{Rem}_{x},\qquad\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}=AA^{\top}+\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}.

Add and subtract Jx​ΣΔ⋆​Jx⊤J_{x}\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}^{\top}:

‖𝒰EΔ−𝒰EBayes‖F≤‖Jx​Cov​(δ​x)​Jx⊤−Jx​ΣΔ⋆​Jx⊤‖F⏟(⋆)+‖Jx​ΣΔ⋆​Jx⊤−A​A⊤‖F⏟Lemma A.9+‖Remx‖F+‖Remθ‖F.\|\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\Delta}-\mathcal{U}_{E}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}\|_{F}\leq\underbrace{\|J_{x}\mathrm{Cov}(\delta x)J_{x}^{\top}-J_{x}\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}^{\top}\|_{F}}_{(\star)}+\underbrace{\|J_{x}\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}J_{x}^{\top}-AA^{\top}\|_{F}}_{\text{Lemma~\ref{lem:bestmatch}}}+\|\mathrm{Rem}_{x}\|_{F}+\|\mathrm{Rem}_{\theta}\|_{F}.

The second term is bounded by Lemma A.9. The remainder terms are bounded as in Steps 1–2. The term (⋆)(\star) vanishes if Cov⁡(δ​x)=ΣΔ⋆\mathrm{Cov}(\delta x)=\Sigma_{\Delta}^{\star}; more generally it is absorbed into the linearization/remainder group (it quantifies mismatch between the actual perturbation covariance and the best-match covariance). Collecting yields (22). ∎

What this gives the main paper. (22) is the εE​(x)\varepsilon_{E}(x) defect bound used in the informal Pillar 2 statement (Thm. 4.2). Reading the right-hand side: the first two terms shrink with the semantic-coverage diagnostic D3 (App. C), while the last remainder shrinks with the linearity diagnostic D1; the bridge is tight precisely when both diagnostics report small values.

A.3.3 Aleatoric bridge via stability of conditional covariance

Assumption A.11 (Lipschitz aleatoric map).

There exist a mapping G:ℝd→𝕊+dG:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d} and constants LG,ρG≥0L_{G},\rho_{G}\geq 0 such that

‖Σθ​(x)−G⁡(mθ​(x))‖F≤ρGfor all (x,θ) in the local neighborhood,\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-G(m_{\theta}(x))\|_{F}\leq\rho_{G}\quad\text{for all $(x,\theta)$ in the local neighborhood,} (23)

and GG is Lipschitz:

‖G⁡(u)−G⁡(v)‖F≤LG​‖u−v‖∀u,v∈ℝd.\|G(u)-G(v)\|_{F}\leq L_{G}\|u-v\|\quad\forall u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (24)
Discussion.

Assumption A.11 formalizes the empirical observation that the within-perturbation dispersion of LLM outputs (decoding stochasticity at a fixed prompt) varies smoothly with the predictive state mθ​(x)m_{\theta}(x) rather than discontinuously. This is consistent with the observation that decoding noise is primarily a function of local entropy of the next-token distribution, which is itself a smooth function of the hidden representation. Both LGL_{G} and ρG\rho_{G} are defect terms: the bridge is tightest when decoding stochasticity is well-approximated by a Lipschitz function of the predictive mean, and the bound (25) degrades gracefully with ρG\rho_{G} rather than breaking. We do not need ρG=0\rho_{G}=0.

Theorem A.12 (Aleatoric bridge bound).

Under Assumption A.11 and the setup of Section 4.2,

‖𝒰AΔ​(x)−𝒰ABayes​(x)‖F≤LG​𝔼​[‖mθ​(x)−mθ⋆​(xΔ)‖]+ 2​ρG,\|\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x)-\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)\|_{F}\;\leq\;L_{G}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\|m_{\theta}(x)-m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|\Big]\;+\;2\rho_{G}, (25)

where the expectation is under any coupling of (θ,Δ)(\theta,\Delta). Moreover, under Assumptions A.6–A.8, one can choose a coupling such that

𝔼⁡[‖mθ​(x)−mθ⋆​(xΔ)‖]≲‖A⁡(x)‖F​εcov​(x)+𝔼​‖rθ‖+𝔼​‖rx‖.\mathbb{E}\Big[\|m_{\theta}(x)-m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|\Big]\;\lesssim\;\|A(x)\|_{F}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}}(x)+\mathbb{E}\|r_{\theta}\|+\mathbb{E}\|r_{x}\|. (26)
Proof.

We provide a detailed proof of (25); the refinement (26) follows by the same best-match argument used in the epistemic bridge.

Step 1: pointwise bound on conditional covariances. Fix (θ,Δ)(\theta,\Delta) and write xΔ=T⁡(x,Δ)x_{\Delta}=T(x,\Delta). By triangle inequality,

‖Σθ​(x)−Σθ⋆​(xΔ)‖F≤‖Σθ​(x)−G⁡(mθ​(x))‖F+‖G⁡(mθ​(x))−G⁡(mθ⋆​(xΔ))‖F+‖G⁡(mθ⋆​(xΔ))−Σθ⋆​(xΔ)‖F.\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|_{F}\leq\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-G(m_{\theta}(x))\|_{F}+\|G(m_{\theta}(x))-G(m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta}))\|_{F}+\|G(m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta}))-\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|_{F}. (27)

Apply Assumption A.11 to the first and third terms to get ≤ρG\leq\rho_{G} each. Apply Lipschitzness (24) to the middle term:

‖G⁡(mθ​(x))−G⁡(mθ⋆​(xΔ))‖F≤LG​‖mθ​(x)−mθ⋆​(xΔ)‖.\|G(m_{\theta}(x))-G(m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta}))\|_{F}\leq L_{G}\|m_{\theta}(x)-m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|.

Thus, for all (θ,Δ)(\theta,\Delta) in the local neighborhood,

‖Σθ​(x)−Σθ⋆​(xΔ)‖F≤LG​‖mθ​(x)−mθ⋆​(xΔ)‖+2​ρG.\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|_{F}\leq L_{G}\|m_{\theta}(x)-m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|+2\rho_{G}.

Step 2: take expectations under a coupling. Let (θ,Δ)(\theta,\Delta) be jointly distributed under any coupling with marginals θ∼p⁡(θ∣𝒟)\theta\sim p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D}) and Δ∼pΔ\Delta\sim p_{\Delta}. Take expectation of the pointwise inequality:

𝔼​‖Σθ​(x)−Σθ⋆​(xΔ)‖F≤LG​𝔼​‖mθ​(x)−mθ⋆​(xΔ)‖+2​ρG.\mathbb{E}\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|_{F}\leq L_{G}\,\mathbb{E}\|m_{\theta}(x)-m_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|+2\rho_{G}.

Step 3: relate to 𝒰ABayes\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}} and 𝒰AΔ\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}. By definition,

𝒰ABayes​(x)=𝔼θ​[Σθ​(x)],𝒰AΔ​(x)=𝔼Δ​[Σθ⋆​(xΔ)].\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\Sigma_{\theta}(x)],\qquad\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}[\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})].

By Jensen and triangle inequality,

‖𝒰ABayes​(x)−𝒰AΔ​(x)‖F=‖𝔼θ​[Σθ​(x)]−𝔼Δ​[Σθ⋆​(xΔ)]‖F≤𝔼​‖Σθ​(x)−Σθ⋆​(xΔ)‖F.\|\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\mathrm{Bayes}}(x)-\mathcal{U}_{A}^{\Delta}(x)\|_{F}=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{\theta}[\Sigma_{\theta}(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}[\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})]\right\|_{F}\leq\mathbb{E}\|\Sigma_{\theta}(x)-\Sigma_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\|_{F}.

Combine with Step 2 to obtain (25).

Step 4: refinement via semantic coverage (sketch). Under Assumption A.6, local linearization provides mθ​(x)≈mθ⋆​(x)+Jθ​δ​θm_{\theta}(x)\approx m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{\theta}\delta\theta and mθ⋆​(xΔ)≈mθ⋆​(x)+Jx​δ​xm_{\theta^{\star}}(x_{\Delta})\approx m_{\theta^{\star}}(x)+J_{x}\delta x. Choosing a coupling that aligns Jx​δ​xJ_{x}\delta x with Jθ​δ​θJ_{\theta}\delta\theta in the sense of Lemma A.9 yields a mean-gap controlled by ‖A‖F​εcov\|A\|_{F}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cov}} plus remainder terms, giving (26). ∎

What this gives the main paper. (25) is the εA​(x)\varepsilon_{A}(x) defect bound used in the informal Pillar 2 statement (Thm. 4.2). Together with (22), the two bounds furnish the right-hand sides of the Pillar 2 inequalities, completing the bridge defect side of the main-paper claim. The MC error side of the same claim was supplied by App. A.2.

A.4 Spurious Determinism: When Consistency-Only UQ Can Fail

Purpose of this subsection. The main paper’s Pillar 3 (Thm. 4.3) claims a class of inputs on which any consistency-only uncertainty estimator ℱcons\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cons}} is exactly 00 while perturbation EU is bounded away from 00. Here we (i) name the class formally: the “spurious determinism” regime where decoding is deterministic given the prompt but the conditional mean varies across semantic-preserving perturbations; and (ii) construct a concrete instance and prove the separation. The argument is intentionally elementary: the value of the result is in isolating a regime, not in the algebra.

This section formalizes a simple failure mode of “consistency-only” uncertainty heuristics that probe only within-prompt variability under repeated decoding. The key phenomenon is spurious determinism: for a fixed prompt instance, the model may be nearly deterministic (hence self-consistent) yet wrong, while semantically equivalent perturbations expose strong sensitivity.

A.4.1 A minimal construction

Let Δ\Delta be a random perturbation and consider Z=e⁡(Y)∈ℝdZ=e(Y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} under the conditional model p(⋅∣xΔ)p(\cdot\mid x_{\Delta}). Assume that for each fixed Δ\Delta, decoding is deterministic:

Z=μ⁡(Δ)a.s. given ​Δ,Z=\mu(\Delta)\quad\text{a.s.\ given }\Delta, (28)

so that Σ⁡(Δ)=Cov⁡(Z∣Δ)=0\Sigma(\Delta)=\mathrm{Cov}(Z\mid\Delta)=0.

Now assume μ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta) varies across Δ\Delta due to a spurious prompt feature. A concrete example: let u,v∈ℝdu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be orthonormal and define

μ⁡(Δ)=a​u+s⁡(Δ)​v,s⁡(Δ)∈{−1,+1},ℙ⁡(s=+1)=ℙ⁡(s=−1)=12,\mu(\Delta)=a\,u+s(\Delta)\,v,\qquad s(\Delta)\in\{-1,+1\},\qquad\mathbb{P}(s=+1)=\mathbb{P}(s=-1)=\tfrac{1}{2}, (29)

where aa is a fixed semantic component and s⁡(Δ)​vs(\Delta)v is a spurious component that flips across perturbations.

Theorem A.13 (Spurious determinism implies UA=0U_{A}=0 but UE≻0U_{E}\succ 0).

Assume (28). Then UA=𝔼Δ​[Σ⁡(Δ)]=0U_{A}=\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}[\Sigma(\Delta)]=0. If μ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta) is non-constant with CovΔ​(μ⁡(Δ))≠0\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta}(\mu(\Delta))\neq 0, then

UE=CovΔ​(μ⁡(Δ))≽0andUE≠0.U_{E}=\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta}(\mu(\Delta))\succcurlyeq 0\quad\text{and}\quad U_{E}\neq 0.

In particular, under the flip model (29),

UE=v​v⊤,tr⁡(UE)=‖v‖22=1.U_{E}=vv^{\top},\qquad\mathrm{tr}(U_{E})=\|v\|_{2}^{2}=1.
Proof.

If Z=μ⁡(Δ)Z=\mu(\Delta) a.s. given Δ\Delta, then Σ⁡(Δ)=Cov⁡(Z∣Δ)=0\Sigma(\Delta)=\mathrm{Cov}(Z\mid\Delta)=0 for every Δ\Delta, so UA=𝔼Δ​[Σ⁡(Δ)]=0U_{A}=\mathbb{E}_{\Delta}[\Sigma(\Delta)]=0.

By definition, UE=CovΔ​(μ⁡(Δ))U_{E}=\mathrm{Cov}_{\Delta}(\mu(\Delta)) is always positive semidefinite. Moreover, UE=0U_{E}=0 iff μ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta) is a.s. constant; thus if μ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta) is non-constant, then UE≠0U_{E}\neq 0.

For the flip model (29), note 𝔼⁡[s⁡(Δ)]=0\mathbb{E}[s(\Delta)]=0 and Var⁡(s)=1\mathrm{Var}(s)=1. Then 𝔼⁡[μ⁡(Δ)]=a​u\mathbb{E}[\mu(\Delta)]=a\,u and

μ⁡(Δ)−𝔼⁡[μ⁡(Δ)]=s⁡(Δ)​v.\mu(\Delta)-\mathbb{E}[\mu(\Delta)]=s(\Delta)\,v.

Therefore,

UE=𝔼⁡[(μ−𝔼​μ)​(μ−𝔼​μ)⊤]=𝔼⁡[s​(Δ)2​v​v⊤]=v​v⊤.U_{E}=\mathbb{E}\big[(\mu-\mathbb{E}\mu)(\mu-\mathbb{E}\mu)^{\top}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[s(\Delta)^{2}\,vv^{\top}\big]=vv^{\top}.

Taking trace yields tr⁡(UE)=tr⁡(v​v⊤)=‖v‖22=1\mathrm{tr}(U_{E})=\mathrm{tr}(vv^{\top})=\|v\|_{2}^{2}=1. ∎

Interpretation. Under spurious determinism, any uncertainty method that only probes within-prompt decoding variability (i.e., only Σ⁡(Δ)\Sigma(\Delta) for a fixed prompt instance) will report near-zero uncertainty, even if the output is highly sensitive to semantic-preserving perturbations. Our perturbation-based epistemic term UEU_{E} is designed to detect precisely this sensitivity.

What this gives the main paper. Theorem A.13 is the formalization of the main paper’s Pillar 3 statement (Thm. 4.3). The class “ℱcons=0\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{cons}}{=}0 but UEU_{E} bounded away from 00” is exactly the spurious-determinism regime constructed above; it has positive measure under any base distribution placing mass on prompt-format-driven outputs, since the flip model is realizable whenever the LLM has a deterministic mode that depends on a non-semantic prompt feature. Empirically, in Sec. 5.4, disambiguating a prompt significantly reduces EU while leaving all fixed-prompt consistency baselines statistically unchanged (Tab. 5).

Appendix B Validating the AU/EU Decomposition: Additional Details

This appendix provides additional setup detail and supplementary results for the controlled diagnostics in Sec. 5.4 of the main paper.

Calibration metric (ECE): definition used throughout the paper.

A raw uncertainty score is not a probability, so a calibration metric requires a mapping to [0,1][0,1]. We use the same protocol in every ECE column reported anywhere in the paper (Tab. 6 main, Tab. 16, Tab. 13, Tab. 15): (i) split the (uncertainty, error-label) pairs 70/3070/30 into evaluation and calibration folds with a fixed seed; (ii) fit a single-feature logistic regression (scikit-learn LogisticRegression() defaults; equivalent to a sigmoid / Platt calibrator) on the calibration fold mapping uncertainty to p^​(error)∈[0,1]\hat{p}(\text{error})\in[0,1]; (iii) apply this map to the evaluation fold; (iv) compute ECE with 1515 equal-width bins on [0,1][0,1], with a left-closed, right-open bin convention except for the final bin which is closed at both ends. The error label is 1−correctness1{-}\text{correctness}, where correctness is the same Cosine or ROUGE-L criterion (or LLM-judge lenient label, for long-form) used in the corresponding AUROC column. We return NaN on degenerate splits (single-class fold). This single procedure yields all reported ECE values.

Datasets and pairing.

For the AmbigQA [36] test we use the public AmbigQA development split, restricted to questions whose ambiguity is annotated and whose gold clarification is a one-sentence rewrite of the question (this excludes free-form clarifying paragraphs). For the NQ evidence test we use the Natural Questions [25] short-answer subset and pair each closed-book question with its gold long answer passage; the long answer is concatenated as additional context but outer perturbations are applied only to the question span, so the perturbation distribution is held fixed across the closed/open conditions.

Statistical procedure.

Per-example AUROC contributions are computed via a Hanley–McNeil-style pairwise formulation: each correct/incorrect pair contributes 𝟙[u−>u+]+12𝟙[u−=u+]\mathbb{1}[u_{-}>u_{+}]+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{1}[u_{-}=u_{+}] to the AUROC (with u+u_{+}/u−u_{-} the uncertainty of the correct/incorrect answer under the incorrect-as-positive convention). The paired statistic Δ​AU−Δ​EU\Delta\mathrm{AU}-\Delta\mathrm{EU} averages these contributions per example before differencing, which removes between-example variance. The zz-statistic in Table 3 is a Wald test on the per-example paired differences using their per-example sample variance; the BCa intervals reported in Table 11 are computed from a paired bootstrap with 1,0001{,}000 resamples, and the same procedure also gives the standard errors in Table 3.

Replication on Qwen2.5-7B.

Table 11 replicates the full 2×22{\times}2 paired-intervention protocol of Table 3 on Qwen2.5-7B under Cosine and ROUGE-L correctness. The predicted decomposition pattern transfers cleanly: clarification on AmbigQA selectively moves AU (ROUGE-L: z=2.44z{=}2.44, p=0.015p{=}0.015; Cosine directional, p=0.125p{=}0.125), and evidence on NQ selectively moves EU (z=9.33z{=}9.33 and z=12.13z{=}12.13, both p<0.001p{<}0.001). The NQ contrasts are substantially larger than the LLaMA-3-8B headline (Δ​EU−Δ​AU=+0.085\Delta\mathrm{EU}\!-\!\Delta\mathrm{AU}{=}+0.085 and +0.110+0.110, vs. +0.030+0.030 and +0.047+0.047 on LLaMA-3-8B), consistent with Qwen’s larger closed-book knowledge gap on NQ being more dramatically closed by evidence injection.

Why bootstrapping rather than reporting raw AUROC differences?

The two intervention conditions share the same examples and only differ in how the input is augmented. Reporting raw between-condition AUROC differences would treat them as independent samples and inflate variance. The paired contrast we report removes this and is valid even though AU and EU AUROCs differ in absolute level.

Score-level shifts and baseline comparisons.

Tab. 5 evaluates raw score changes across the exact question pairs of Tab. 3. Fixed-prompt baselines (embedding variance, self-consistency, discrete semantic entropy, and uniform Semantic Density) are computed from 1010 stochastic decodes of the prompt per condition, SPUQ is computed from 1010 single-decode perturbations per condition (temperature 0.90.9, top-pp 0.990.99), and our AU/EU/TU components use the N=M=10N{=}M{=}10 runs. For each question pair, we compute the paired difference δ=scoreafter−scorebefore\delta=\text{score}_{\text{after}}-\text{score}_{\text{before}} and report the standardized shift δ¯/sd⁡(δ)\bar{\delta}/\mathrm{sd}(\delta); statistical significance (bold in Tab. 5) means that the 95%95\% percentile bootstrap confidence interval of δ¯\bar{\delta} (over 5,0005{,}000 resamples of question pairs) excludes zero. On an absolute scale, our EU decreases by −7.6×10−5-7.6{\times}10^{-5} (95%95\% CI [−9.8,−5.5]×10−5[-9.8,-5.5]{\times}10^{-5}) under clarification, relative to a pre-intervention mean of 5.5×10−45.5{\times}10^{-4}.

Bias correction.

The bias-correction validation is at the score level (AU–EU correlation ρ\rho) and is reported in main-paper Table 5 on the TriviaQA/LLaMA-3-8B/Cosine slice. We do not include an additional appendix table because ρ\rho is the right object for the finite-MM inflation predicted by Prop. 4.1: the correction acts on the uncertainty score itself, not on downstream AUROC.

Appendix C Bridge Diagnostics: Estimating Assumption Quality from Data

The Bayesian bridge in Sec. 4 closes the gap between perturbation-based AU/EU and Bayesian targets only under Assumption A.6 (local first-order linearization of the conditional mean), Assumption A.7 (locally Gaussian posterior), and Assumption A.8 (bounded semantic coverage defect). This appendix turns each assumption into a diagnostic that is estimable from data, and reports its value on our datasets.

Local linearity defect (Assumption A.6 diagnostic).

For a perturbation neighborhood 𝒩ε​(x)\mathcal{N}_{\varepsilon}(x), define the linearity defect LD⁡(x,ε):=‖f⁡(x+Δ)−f⁡(x)−Jx​Δ‖/‖Δ‖\mathrm{LD}(x;\varepsilon):=\|f(x+\Delta)-f(x)-J_{x}\Delta\|/\|\Delta\|, where JxJ_{x} is the embedding-space slope of ff estimated by least squares on {(Δi,f⁡(x+Δi))}i=1N\{(\Delta_{i},f(x+\Delta_{i}))\}_{i=1}^{N}. The bridge bound depends on 𝔼⁡[LD2]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{LD}^{2}], which is directly measurable from the same outer-perturbation samples already collected for the AU/EU estimator. We report per-input mean, standard deviation, and 95th percentile of LD⁡(x,ε)\mathrm{LD}(x;\varepsilon).

Posterior Gaussianity (Assumption A.7 diagnostic).

Assumption A.7 is a Laplace approximation on parameters (δ​θ∼𝒩⁡(0,Σθ)\delta\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{\theta})); under the local linearity in Assumption A.6, this induces an approximately Gaussian distribution on embeddings. We therefore test the induced embedding distribution directly. (We do not test scalar uncertainty scores; HZ on a one-dimensional summary would be a different test of a different object and is not what the bridge requires.) Two multivariate clouds in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d=384d{=}384) are available per input: (a) the outer-mean cloud {μ^i​(x)}i=1N\{\hat{\mu}_{i}(x)\}_{i=1}^{N} across the N=10N{=}10 perturbations: this is the cloud most directly tied to Assumption A.7, since under linearity it is the pushforward of δ​θ\delta\theta via JθJ_{\theta}; and (b) the inner-sample cloud {zi,j​(x)}j=1M\{z_{i,j}(x)\}_{j=1}^{M} across the M=10M{=}10 stochastic decodes at fixed perturbation, which probes within-perturbation aleatoric Gaussianity (a side condition used in the AU bridge). The HZ column in Table 12 reports the rejection rate of test (b), which is the better-powered of the two: with only N=M=10N{=}M{=}10 samples in d=384d{=}384, both forms of the test are deeply underpowered, and on the per-input outer-mean cloud (test (a)) the average pp-value collapses to numerical zero (∼10−14\sim\!10^{-14} on all four cells), reflecting the test’s high-dimensional small-sample behavior under our budget; the HZ statistic is reported as a Gaussianity diagnostic alongside LD and MMD, and the load-bearing diagnostic for the bridge bound itself is LD.

Coverage diagnostic (perturbation–reference MMD).

The semantic coverage defect that enters the bridge bound is, in principle, a Wasserstein distance between the empirical perturbation distribution and a Bayesian posterior over inputs the model treats equivalently. The latter is not directly observable; we report instead the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in embedding space, computed with a Gaussian RBF kernel and median-heuristic bandwidth, between the embedded perturbation cloud and a held-out 1,0001{,}000-prompt reference distribution from the same dataset. This quantity measures how close the perturbation cloud sits to in-distribution prompts in the same semantic neighborhood; small values indicate that the outer perturbation distribution covers the relevant semantic geometry rather than drifting elsewhere.

What the diagnostics imply for the bridge bound.

Substituting the empirical LD into the bridge defect bound in Theorem 4.2 yields end-to-end excess terms εE,εA\varepsilon_{E},\varepsilon_{A} on the perturbation-population covariance (Frobenius norm) that are dominated by the LD-squared contribution. With 𝔼⁡[LD2]≤(0.27)2+(0.10)2≈0.083\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{LD}^{2}]\leq(0.27)^{2}+(0.10)^{2}\approx 0.083 in the worst cell (Qwen2.5-7B/TruthfulQA), the bridge contributes a small fraction of the perturbation-population covariance norm in the limit N,M→∞N,M\to\infty. The Frobenius bound translates to an AUROC perturbation bound under additional ranking-margin / Lipschitz-of-aggregator assumptions; here we focus on the covariance bound that the perturbation framework directly delivers. The HZ rejection rate does not enter this calculation: the bridge bound requires only the second-moment covariance of the embedding distribution to be well-estimated, and the coverage MMD diagnostic absorbs the second-moment relaxation.

Input sensitivity is a meaningful EU signal.

A standard worry is that perturbation-based EU only measures input sensitivity rather than parameter uncertainty. Output variation under input perturbation is in fact a well-studied proxy for epistemic uncertainty [49]: when a model has learned a robust mapping, semantic-preserving perturbations leave the conditional mean μΔ​(x)\mu_{\Delta}(x) approximately fixed; in under-determined regions μΔ​(x)\mu_{\Delta}(x) shifts substantially. Our framework absorbs surface-form variation into AU (Sec. 3), though EU can also capture residual semantic drift when an imperfect paraphrase alters question meaning (audited in App. F.2.3).

Instruction perturbations as parameter perturbations.

Beyond input-content perturbations, prior work shows that in-context tokens (including instructions and formatting) induce implicit gradient updates to the model’s attention parameters [7]. Concretely, processing an in-context update at a fixed weight matrix WW is equivalent to processing the original input under W+Δ​WICLW+\Delta W_{\text{ICL}}, with Δ​WICL\Delta W_{\text{ICL}} a low-rank parameter shift induced by the in-context tokens. Under this interpretation, instruction-style outer perturbations fall inside the bridge: the perturbation operates on effective parameters (θ+Δ​θICL\theta+\Delta\theta_{\text{ICL}}), so an analogous bridge argument applies with the induced parameter-shift covariance replacing the input-side covariance. This perspective explains, rather than contradict, the empirical observation that instruction-style perturbations yield a strong EU signal in our ablations: under [7], instruction variation acts directly as an implicit parameter perturbation rather than a mere surface-form confound.

Appendix D SPUQ Comparison and Aggregation Factorization

SPUQ [13] is the closest published black-box method and shares two ingredients with our method (input perturbations and sampled answers), but differs in three structural ways: (a) one level vs. two levels — SPUQ takes one decode per perturbation, so the conditional moments μΔ,ΣΔ\mu_{\Delta},\Sigma_{\Delta} that the law of total covariance requires are unavailable, and no AU/EU split is even definable; (b) scalar vs. matrix-valued — SPUQ’s aggregators collapse the perturbation cloud into one number, while we return (U^A,U^E)∈ℝd×d×ℝd×d(\widehat{U}_{A},\widehat{U}_{E})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\!\times\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} with the predicted finite-MM bias correction, which is what enables the paired interventions in Sec. 5.4; (c) heuristic vs. analyzed — SPUQ provides no theoretical analysis of consistency or bias, while Prop. A.1 and Thm. A.5 cover both and the separation result formalizes a class of failures that fixed-prompt consistency scores provably miss.

Head-to-head comparison.

We operate our method at N=M=10N{=}M{=}10 to share the outer perturbation count (KSPUQ=N=10K_{\mathrm{SPUQ}}{=}N{=}10) with SPUQ; ours additionally incurs M=10M{=}10 inner decodes per outer perturbation, which is the intrinsic cost of the two-level decomposition and is not present in any one-level method. This is not a matched total-API-call budget (ours uses ∼10×\sim\!10\times more LLM calls per input; equal budgets: Tab. 2); we read the comparison as “does the decomposition deliver capability the one-level scalar cannot, and is the gain large enough to justify the extra inner decodes?”. Table 13 reports the {\{LLaMA-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B}×{\}\!\times\!\{TriviaQA, TruthfulQA}\} result. Three observations: (i) Ours (TU) dominates SPUQ (TU) on all four cells, with the largest gap on Qwen2.5-7B / TruthfulQA where SPUQ drops to 0.3920.392 (worse than chance) while our TU stays at 0.6290.629; (ii) Ours (AU) is uniformly the strongest single column (0.6300.630–0.8550.855); (iii) calibration favors ours on TriviaQA by a 44–8×8\times margin (TU ECE 0.0130.013–0.0150.015 vs. 0.0620.062–0.1040.104) and is essentially tied on TruthfulQA, so there is no calibration cost to the two-level structure. The next subsection isolates which structural difference is load-bearing.

The perturbation family is not the load-bearing piece.

A natural follow-up question is whether our gain over SPUQ comes simply from using a better perturbation. Table 24 ablates the perturbation family while holding the two-level structure fixed: the framework works with random paraphrasing, distractor injection, instruction variation, and SPUQ-style noise, with instruction variation giving the best signal.

D.1 Decomposition vs. aggregator: a 2×22{\times}2 factorial

We isolate which structural difference is load-bearing by replacing our embedding-statistics aggregator with SPUQ’s [13] inter-sample (pairwise) ROUGE-L [30] aggregator while keeping the two-level ensemble structure unchanged. The four conditions form a 2×22{\times}2 factorial along the decomposition axis (one-level vs. two-level) and the aggregator axis (ROUGE-L vs. embedding-statistics): (i) one-level + ROUGE aggregator (vanilla SPUQ); (ii) one-level + embedding aggregator; (iii) two-level + ROUGE aggregator; (iv) two-level + embedding aggregator (our full method). One-level conditions emit a single TU score and have no AU/EU split; two-level conditions expose AU, EU, TU and the AU–EU per-example Spearman correlation.

Calibration corollary.

The two-level ++ embedding configuration also has materially lower TU expected calibration error than the alternatives on the cosine-correctness slice: TU ECE is 0.0150.015 (LLaMA-3-8B / TriviaQA) and 0.0130.013 (Qwen2.5-7B / TriviaQA) for (iv), versus 0.0660.066 and 0.0530.053 for (iii) and 0.0710.071 and 0.0650.065 for (i). On TruthfulQA all four conditions have TU ECE below 0.0110.011, dominated by base-rate effects. This pattern is consistent with the AU–EU ρ\rho result: ROUGE-L scalars carry duplicate information across both heads and so overconfide, whereas the embedding-statistics decomposition produces uncertainty heads that are individually well-calibrated.

Reading the result.

The gain over SPUQ has two distinct structural sources, both load-bearing. Table 14 attributes them: the two-level decomposition supplies the AUROC gain, and the embedding-statistics aggregator supplies the AU/EU separation that makes the decomposition usable downstream (Sec. 5.4). Replacing only one factor leaves the other capability missing: configuration (iii) matches us on AU AUROC but cannot tell AU from EU, and configuration (ii) has clean scoring geometry but no decomposition to apply it to.

Robustness across correctness criteria.

The headline table reports cosine-thresholded correctness on the two-level conditions only. Table 15 mirrors it under both Cosine and ROUGE-L correctness: the AU AUROC of (iii) and (iv) stays within 0.030.03, and the calibration advantage of the embedding aggregator on TriviaQA persists across both criteria.

Appendix E Long-form Pilot: Segment-level UQ on NQ Long-Answer

The main-paper claim-level result is in Tab. 6. This appendix provides (a) the full pipeline specification (§E.1), (b) the response-level companion table (Tab. 16), and (c) the discussion of the pilot’s scope and conclusions. Setup recap: we apply our method to long-form generation on the NQ long-answer split [25], in two complementary granularities: response-level, treating the full long answer as one unit and reporting both mean- and max-aggregation of the per-sentence segment scores; and claim-level (main paper), decomposing each long answer into atomic claims (using a same-strength LLM extractor) and scoring each claim independently. Correctness is judged by an LLM judge against the gold long-answer paragraph; we use the lenient judge variant at response level (the strict variant returned no fully-correct response in this small pilot, which is itself diagnostic) and a per-claim factuality label at claim level. The five black-box baselines (avgEntail, NonContradiction, UQLM cosine following Bouchard et al. [5], Ross et al. [47], SelfCheckGPT [35], and ROUGE-L (cons.) [30]) consume the same per-claim M=5M{=}5 inner sample pool that our method uses; this gives every consistency-only baseline exactly the budget it can use (the inner level), so the comparison is on equal terms for the slot they occupy.
