Within the n=100n{=}100/∼103\sim\!10^{3}-claim setup with an LLM-judge factuality label, the pilot supports three concrete conclusions: (1) the two-level decomposition transports to claim-level long-form factuality without retraining, beating surface-similarity baselines on both models and trailing a pretrained NLI scorer (avgEntail) by 0.0090.009 on LLaMA-3-8B and 0.0600.060 on Qwen2.5-7B; (2) the AU >> EU ordering is preserved at long-form, mirroring the short-form behavior; (3) the framework and entailment-based scorers are complementary, motivating a hybrid that retains the two-level outer perturbation structure with an NLI-based inner aggregator. The bias-correction identity (Prop. 4.1) is derived for short-form and would be re-derived for the long-form variant in such a hybrid. Response- and claim-level results are in Tab. 16 and main-paper Tab. 6.

Appendix F Ablation Studies

Large-model results. Table 17 reports results for larger instruction-tuned models (70B+), which are often more capable but may also display different calibration behavior. We include these results to demonstrate that the relative trends between our AU/EU/TU decomposition and competing baselines remain consistent at larger model scales.

F.1 Sampling budget: two-level ensemble sizes (NN, MM)

Appendix Tables 18,19, 19(b) study sensitivity to the two-level ensemble budget, where the outer size NN controls the number of semantic perturbation draws and the inner size MM controls the number of within-input stochastic generations per perturbation. The main-text Tab. 7(b) shows a compressed view (TruthfulQA, Cosine) of the tied-budget sweep; the full grid is in Table 18. We report: (i) tied budgets N=MN{=}M (Table 18), (ii) fixed outer ensemble N=10N{=}10 with varying MM (Table 19), and (iii) fixed inner ensemble M=10M{=}10 with varying NN (Table 19(b)). We additionally provide wall-clock measurements in seconds per question for representative budgets (Table 20).

Empirical trend: rapid improvement then plateau. Across TruthfulQA and TriviaQA, performance improves quickly from very small budgets and then exhibits diminishing returns. For tied budgets (Table 18), 3→53{\to}5 yields large gains on TruthfulQA (especially AU/TU under Cosine), while 10→20−3010{\to}20{-}30 provides only marginal improvement; the same pattern holds along single axes (Tables 19, 19(b)). Overall, (N,M)≈(10,10)(N,M){\approx}(10,10) is a strong default that achieves near-peak AUROC while remaining computationally practical.

Why plateauing is expected, and what small budgets miss. The AU/EU/TU estimates are Monte Carlo approximations under two sources of randomness: within-input stochasticity (inner sampling, 1/M1/M) and across-perturbation diversity (outer sampling, 1/N1/N). Once estimation noise drops below the irreducible overlap between correct/incorrect score distributions, improvements taper. Caveat: good AUROC at very small budgets does not imply sufficient uncertainty coverage — the estimator may approximate the mean well yet miss low-probability modes (paraphrase neighborhoods that trigger hallucination, decoding branches with inconsistent claims). Thus N=M=3N{=}M{=}3 is a reasonable AUROC starting point but a low-diversity regime for hard cases.

Interpreting NN vs. MM and practical recipe. MM primarily reduces noise in within-perturbation statistics (relevant for AU); NN expands across-perturbation coverage (relevant for EU because EU is driven by variability across semantically nearby prompts). Both axes improve TU, but the decomposition gives an operational handle: spend more on MM when decoding stochasticity dominates, more on NN when semantic instability dominates. Runtime grows as ∝N​M\propto NM (Table 20); (N,M)≈(10,10)(N,M){\approx}(10,10) delivers near-peak AUROC at ∼1.8\sim\!1.8 sec/question, while (20−30)(20{-}30) budgets are worth the cost only when tail coverage matters more than average performance.

F.1.1 Matched total generation budget

Tab. 2 compares alternative allocations of a fixed per-question generation budget B∈{10,25,100}B\in\{10,25,100\} across the same 400400 TriviaQA questions per model, using the main-paper decoding hyperparameters, Sentence-BERT encoder, and Exact Match (EM) correctness labels. Fixed prompt: BB decodes subsampled from 100100 stochastic generations of the unperturbed prompt, from which embedding variance, self-consistency, discrete semantic entropy, and Semantic Density [42] are computed. Perturbation-only: BB distinct paraphrases with a single decode each (N=B,M=1N{=}B,M{=}1), where finite-MM bias correction is inapplicable. Decoupled: an unnested split of ⌊B/2⌋\lfloor B/2\rfloor fixed-prompt decodes and ⌈B/2⌉\lceil B/2\rceil single-decode paraphrases with summed variances. Ours: nested allocations of N×M=5×2N{\times}M=5{\times}2, 5×55{\times}5 (subsampled from the 10×1010{\times}10 runs), and 10×1010{\times}10. At B=10B{=}10, the one-level perturbation designs draw from the primary paraphrase pool, whereas at B≥25B{\geq}25 they draw from an extended pool. SPUQ cycles through its three perturbation modes (paraphrasing, dummy tokens, and system-prompt variation) with one decode per perturbed prompt (temperature 0.90.9, top-pp 0.990.99), subsampling B=25B{=}25 and B=100B{=}100 from 100100 total generations. Likelihood-weighted Semantic Density incorporates teacher-forced sequence log-probabilities over the fixed-prompt responses. Tabs. 21 and 22 report the complete results with bootstrap 95%95\% confidence intervals, including the individual decoupled terms and our standalone EU component.

F.1.2 Adaptive per-question stopping

To reduce inference overhead on easy or unambiguous queries, the sampling budget can be adapted dynamically per question. We evaluate a sequential stopping rule over the 10×1010{\times}10 runs by computing bias-corrected TU across nested prefixes of size 3×33{\times}3, 5×55{\times}5, 7×77{\times}7, and 10×1010{\times}10 (99, 2525, 4949, and 100100 generations), estimating its relative standard error via a jackknife over the outer perturbations, and halting at the earliest prefix where the relative SE falls below 0.20.2. Across all four model–dataset cells (LLaMA-3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B on TriviaQA and TruthfulQA, 400400 questions each), this rule reduces the median cost to 2525 generations (mean 4646–5353, with 3232–43%43\% of queries proceeding to 10×1010{\times}10). On TriviaQA (EM label), early stopping incurs an AUROC drop of at most 0.0140.014 on LLaMA-3-8B and 0.0010.001 on Qwen2.5-7B relative to the full 10×1010{\times}10 budget, while maintaining per-question Spearman rank correlations of 0.9460.946 and 0.9430.943 (and at least 0.910.91 across all four cells).

F.2 Perturbation design and noise sensitivity

Appendix Table 24 evaluates alternative perturbation mechanisms on TruthfulQA, while Appendix Table 23 varies the outer perturbation magnitude (embedding noise scale ε\varepsilon). Together, they support two conclusions: (i) our framework is not brittle to a single perturbation implementation and remains effective across several families (including non-embedding perturbations), and (ii) perturbations must strike a balance between diversity (to expose instability) and semantic validity (to avoid introducing novelty).

F.2.1 Noise level (perturbation magnitude): diversity–validity trade-off

Varying ε\varepsilon reveals a clear diversity–validity sweet spot (Appendix Table 23). At very small noise (ε∈{0.01,0.02}\varepsilon\in\{0.01,0.02\}), AUROC is modest and often unstable across metrics, consistent with insufficient diversity: perturbations remain too close to the original input in embedding space, producing limited behavioral change and weak separability. At moderate noise (ε≈0.05​–​0.2\varepsilon\approx 0.05\text{--}0.2), AU and TU improve under the Cosine criterion, indicating that the perturbations explore a sufficiently rich local neighborhood to probe uncertainty-relevant variability while largely preserving intent. However, pushing noise too far (ε≥0.5\varepsilon\geq 0.5) causes a sharp collapse for all three uncertainties, especially under ROUGE-L, which is consistent with semantic invalidity: perturbations begin to introduce novelty that breaks the “intent-preserving” assumption and degrades correctness prediction.

Importantly, the mismatch between Cosine and ROUGE-L at larger ε\varepsilon is itself diagnostic: embedding-based proximity can remain high even when surface-level overlap deteriorates, so ROUGE-L drops earlier and more severely. This suggests that, in practice, ε\varepsilon should be tuned to remain within a regime where both semantic similarity and task intent are stable, rather than maximizing exploration alone. Overall, these trends are consistent with the perturbation–Bayesian bridge intuition: we want perturbations that are strong enough to reveal meaningful local sensitivity, but not so strong that they leave the local validity regime.

Scaling of AU and EU magnitudes with perturbation noise ε\varepsilon.

Evaluating the estimator across seven noise scales (ε∈{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0}\varepsilon\in\{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0\} on LLaMA-3-8B across 817817 TruthfulQA questions) directly tests how each component responds to perturbation magnitude. Within the local regime ε∈[0.01,0.2]\varepsilon\in[0.01,0.2], mean EU grows nearly linearly with ε\varepsilon (R2=0.978R^{2}{=}0.978, rising from 3.7×10−53.7{\times}10^{-5} to 6.2×10−46.2{\times}10^{-4}), and the per-question Spearman correlation between EU and ε\varepsilon is positive for 100%100\% of questions across all seven scales (median ρ=0.93\rho{=}0.93). By contrast, mean AU shifts by only 2.3%2.3\% over ε∈[0.01,0.2]\varepsilon\in[0.01,0.2] and exhibits no monotonic trend across the full sweep (positive per-question correlation on 52%52\% of questions), confirming that ε\varepsilon selectively scales between-perturbation EU while leaving within-prompt AU virtually invariant.

F.2.2 Noise type (perturbation mechanism)

Appendix Table 24 shows that the proposed estimator remains competitive across multiple perturbation families, including distractor injection, paraphrase-based perturbations, and SPUQ-style noise [13]. This indicates that the performance gains are driven by structured perturbation diversity in general, not by a single hand-picked recipe.

Among the tested families, instruction variation performs best and most consistently across AU/EU/TU and both correctness criteria. In contrast, paraphrase perturbations exhibit a more mixed pattern: Top-kk paraphrases (the kk nearest neighbors of e⁡(x)e(x) inside the pool) can strengthen EU under Cosine, but can be less reliable under ROUGE-L, consistent with occasional semantic drift and surface-form mismatch. Distractor injection is competitive but less stable, plausibly because distractors introduce extra semantics that may violate intent preservation. Overall, these results reinforce that perturbations should preserve task intent while inducing sufficient surface-form diversity; methods that reliably satisfy both criteria yield the cleanest uncertainty signal.

This is a notable (and useful) stress test: instruction variation changes how the task is asked while keeping the underlying question content fixed. As a result, it does not align perfectly with our primary theoretical lens of “input-content perturbations” in a local semantic neighborhood. Nevertheless, its strong empirical effect suggests an additional, distinct axis of uncertainty: spurious prompt factors (wording, format, persona, constraints) can act like “domains” that modulate model behavior even when content is unchanged. From this perspective, instruction variation can be viewed as sampling over a latent nuisance variable (prompt domain), analogous to marginalizing over domain shifts in domain generalization; it implicitly probes a broader posterior over behaviors than content-only perturbations. Formalizing this connection (e.g., treating prompt style/instructions as a spurious factor and relating variation across instruction domains to a posterior-style term, in the spirit of p⁡(θ∣D)p(\theta\mid D)) is outside the scope of our current bridge assumptions, but is a promising direction for extending black-box UQ beyond content perturbations.

F.2.3 Semantic validity audit of outer perturbations

Ideal outer perturbations should preserve a question’s semantic meaning, ground-truth answer, and level of specificity. We audit all 1010 selected perturbations across 200200 questions per dataset (2,0002{,}000 prompt–perturbation pairs each on TruthfulQA and TriviaQA) using two complementary automated evaluators: (1) an NLI-and-entity filter requiring bidirectional NLI entailment alongside exact preservation of numerals, named entities, and reference answers; and (2) an LLM judge (Qwen3.6-27B) scoring meaning, answer invariance, and clarity on a 11–55 scale (passing pairs require ≥4\geq 4 on all three criteria). The NLI-and-entity filter passes 53.4%53.4\% (95%95\% CI [51.2,55.5][51.2,55.5]) of TruthfulQA pairs and 37.7%37.7\% ([35.6,39.8][35.6,39.8]) of TriviaQA pairs, while the LLM judge passes 54.8%54.8\% and 45.9%45.9\%, respectively.

To calibrate the automated checks, three human raters independently evaluated 100100 pairs on the same three criteria via blind forms (without access to automated scores), stratified by the LLM judge’s minimum rating (3434 pairs with minimum ≥4\geq 4, 3333 with minimum 33, and 3333 with minimum ≤2\leq 2). Inter-rater reliability is high: Fleiss’ κ=0.751\kappa{=}0.751 on binary pass/fail (82%82\% unanimous agreement) and mean pairwise quadratic-weighted κ\kappa of 0.900.90, 0.860.86, and 0.860.86 for meaning, answer, and clarity. Under majority vote, 62%62\% of sampled pairs pass (94%94\%, 67%67\%, and 24%24\% across the three strata), yielding an inverse-probability-weighted pass rate of 60%60\% across all 4,0004{,}000 pairs (63%63\% on TruthfulQA, 57%57\% on TriviaQA). Both automated evaluators achieve 68%68\% agreement with the human majority vote (95%95\% CI [58,76][58,76]).

To evaluate sensitivity to paraphrase quality, we recompute both components on TriviaQA using only audit-passing perturbations, which shifts AU and EU AUROCs by at most 0.060.06 (Tab. 25). Furthermore, in a controlled sensitivity test on TruthfulQA (LLaMA-3-8B, 400400 questions, N=M=10N{=}M{=}10) where 11 or 22 of the 1010 outer perturbations per question are replaced by meaning-altering rewrites (entity substitution, negation, or altered constraints), per-question EU rankings maintain Spearman correlations of 0.9470.947 (one replaced) and 0.8990.899 (two replaced) with the clean run.

F.3 Aggregation methods (vector-to-scalar reduction)

Our uncertainty estimators produce vector-valued dispersion signals (e.g., per-dimension variance in embedding space) that must be reduced to a scalar for ranking and AUROC evaluation. Appendix Table 26 compares four simple aggregation rules (mean, sum, max, and ℓ2\ell_{2} norm) for mapping a variance vector to a scalar score.

Overall, performance is consistent across aggregations: AU and TU vary only mildly, indicating that our framework is not sensitive to a particular reduction choice and that the uncertainty signal is broadly distributed rather than being an artifact of one hand-picked scalarization. This robustness is desirable in practice because it suggests that the correctness signal is present under multiple reasonable summaries of dispersion.

Notably, the max aggregator performs best for EU (and also yields the strongest TU) under both correctness criteria. A plausible explanation is that epistemic effects on TruthfulQA are often sparse but sharp: when the model encounters a knowledge gap or a brittle reasoning step, disagreement concentrates along a small number of semantic directions (embedding dimensions) corresponding to specific missing facts or incompatible interpretations. In such cases, mean/sum/norm dilute the peak disagreement by averaging over many dimensions that remain stable, whereas max preserves the most informative “worst-case” direction and thus improves separability. This aligns with the role of EU as a measure of model uncertainty induced by model inadequacy rather than diffuse ambiguity: EU may manifest as localized spikes in representational variance rather than a uniform spread.

In contrast, AU (and TU) are less sensitive to the choice of aggregator, consistent with ambiguity producing broader, more distributed dispersion across semantic dimensions. Taken together, these results suggest a practical guideline: max is a strong default when prioritizing EU-driven hallucination detection on knowledge-intensive QA, while mean/sum/norm offer comparable behavior and can be preferred when a smoother, less aggressive uncertainty profile is desired.

F.4 Paraphrase-pool encoder ablation

Our method relies on a sentence embedding model [45] for two roles: (i) constructing the paraphrase pool and retrieving semantically close perturbations, and (ii) scoring generation correctness via embedding-based similarity. Appendix Table 27 varies this embedding backbone on TruthfulQA (LLaMA-3-8B).

Two patterns stand out. First, performance is reasonably stable across several widely used sentence encoders: AU and TU remain in a similar range for most choices, indicating that the overall framework does not hinge on a single embedding implementation. This robustness is important because it suggests our uncertainty signal arises from the model’s behavioral variability under perturbations, rather than from a brittle similarity metric.

Second, the choice of embedding model materially affects EU, and the best backbone is paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2, which achieves the strongest AU/EU/TU under both Cosine and ROUGE-L criteria. A plausible explanation is alignment between the embedding geometry and the perturbation family: our paraphrase pool is explicitly designed to preserve intent while varying surface form, so embeddings trained for paraphrase identification produce a geometry where (a) semantically equivalent variants cluster tightly and (b) subtle semantic drift is more reliably reflected as distance. This improves both retrieval quality (the “semantic neighborhood” is cleaner) and the correctness proxy (similarity reflects meaning rather than lexical overlap), which in turn reduces noise in the decomposition and strengthens EU separability.

In contrast, retrieval-oriented encoders (e.g., multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1) are optimized for question–answer matching and may underweight stylistic or entailment-preserving paraphrase structure, leading to noisier neighborhoods and weaker correctness prediction. Likewise, very compact general-purpose encoders (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2) may compress fine-grained distinctions needed for separating epistemic effects on a challenging factual dataset like TruthfulQA, resulting in larger variance across runs.

Overall, this ablation suggests a practical guideline: use paraphrase-specialized sentence encoders when the perturbation family is paraphrase-based, since they provide the most faithful local semantic neighborhoods and the cleanest signal for uncertainty decomposition: this is especially true for EU, which is more sensitive to noise in semantic scoring than AU.

F.5 Covariance-encoder ablation

The previous subsection varied the encoder used to retrieve the paraphrase pool. Here we instead vary the encoder e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) used to compute the embedding-space covariance, while keeping the perturbation pool fixed. This separates the encoder’s role in our pipeline (geometry indexer for the embedding-space covariance) from the LLM’s role (source of the AU signal), and tests how much of the AU signal travels with the LLM rather than the encoder.

We re-encode the same generations under three off-the-shelf sentence encoders (Sentence-BERT [45] (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), MPNet (all-mpnet-base-v2), and BGE-base (BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5)), and report (i) AU AUROC per encoder under both correctness criteria (Table 28), and (ii) the per-example Spearman rank correlation of AU scores across encoder pairs (Table 29).

Per-encoder AUROC.

Table 28 shows that absolute AU AUROC moves only modestly across encoders within the same (model, dataset, correctness) cell. On TriviaQA, the worst-encoder vs. best-encoder AU AUROC gap is ≤0.005\leq 0.005 on either model under cosine; on TruthfulQA the spread is larger (≤0.053\leq 0.053 on LLaMA-3-8B, ≤0.02\leq 0.02 on Qwen2.5-7B, with BGE underperforming Sentence-BERT/MPNet) but the qualitative ordering does not change.

Cross-encoder rank stability.

A stronger statement is that the per-example AU ranking our method produces is preserved across encoders. Table 29 reports the Spearman rank correlation of per-example AU scores between encoder pairs. All off-diagonal correlations exceed 0.950.95 on both datasets and both models. This means a downstream consumer of our scores (e.g., abstention thresholds, selective evaluation) gets nearly the same AU ranking regardless of encoder choice, even where absolute AUROC shifts by a few points.

Reading the result.

Two axes pin down the encoder’s contribution to AU: (a) absolute AU AUROC moves only a few points across encoders within any given (model, dataset, correctness) cell; and (b) per-example AU rankings are essentially preserved (ρ≥0.955\rho\geq 0.955 in every cell of Table 29). Different encoders index the embedding-space geometry differently in absolute terms but rank the same inputs in the same order. AU is therefore a property of the underlying LLM that the encoder indexes rather than produces.

F.6 Paraphrase pool size (KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}}).

The short-form experiments use Kpool=500K_{\mathrm{pool}}{=}500 (App. Tab. 33; the long-form pilot uses 5050); the values below are an ablation supporting a compute-efficient Kpool≈50K_{\mathrm{pool}}{\approx}50 recommendation when pool construction is the bottleneck. We hold the two-level sampling budget fixed at N=M=10N{=}M{=}10 and vary KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}}.

Coverage–purity trade-off with intermediate optimum. Results exhibit a clear intermediate optimum rather than monotonic gains: moderate pool sizes (Kpool≈20−100K_{\mathrm{pool}}\!\approx\!20{-}100) are consistently strong, with peak TU at Kpool=50K_{\mathrm{pool}}{=}50 under both similarity criteria, while very small pools underperform (narrow semantic support, repeated anchors) and very large pools degrade AU/TU (nearest-neighbor retrieval picks up “nearby-but-wrong” anchors as the candidate set grows, injecting noise). EU is the exception: it can stay competitive or improve at Kpool=200K_{\mathrm{pool}}{=}200/10001000 under Cosine, consistent with EU benefiting from broader semantic diversity even when the AU/TU decomposition gets noisier. Practical recipe: Kpool≈50K_{\mathrm{pool}}\!\approx\!50 (or 20−10020{-}100) for fixed (N,M)=(10,10)(N,M){=}(10,10); larger pools are worth it only with stronger semantic filtering to prevent drift.

F.7 Temperature stability: TT as a deployment parameter, not an estimator knob

Purpose. The decoding temperature TT shapes the model’s conditional output distribution p(⋅∣x)p(\cdot\!\mid\!x) that all black-box uncertainty estimators sample from. Unlike the perturbation noise scale ε\varepsilon, which is set by our procedure, TT is an internal property of the deployed LLM that we (and any black-box user) treat as fixed. To verify that this fixed-deployment view is benign for the AU/EU decomposition, we run a focused TT-sweep on TruthfulQA.

Setup.

LLaMA-3-8B, TruthfulQA, N=M=10N{=}M{=}10, ε=0.1\varepsilon{=}0.1, Sentence-BERT embedding, Cosine correctness criterion. We sweep T∈{0.3,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.5}T\!\in\!\{0.3,0.7,0.9,1.1,1.5\} (Tab. 31) and report two stability indicators: (i) EU AUROC for correctness prediction, and (ii) the Wasserstein-1 distance between the empirical EU distributions at TT and at the reference T=0.9T{=}0.9.

What this lets us conclude.

Within a sensible deployment range, swapping TT does not meaningfully shift either the EU AUROC or the empirical EU distribution, supporting the fixed-deployment framing in the main paper (Sec. 5). This is in contrast to ε\varepsilon, where moving outside the moderate-perturbation regime our theory targets does shift uncertainty rankings (see noise-level ablation, App. Tab. 23).

Appendix G Qualitative Examples: Ambiguity vs. Knowledge, and When Perturbations Beat Consistency

This appendix provides a small set of representative qualitative examples from TruthfulQA illustrating the intended semantics of our two-level decomposition: aleatoric uncertainty (AU) reflects input-level ambiguity / underspecification (multiple plausible completions under the same intent), while epistemic uncertainty (EU) reflects model knowledge / sensitivity (instability of the predicted semantic mean under intent-preserving perturbations). Rather than listing all examples, we curate a few cases that most directly support these two claims.

Reading guide. For each example we report percentile/rank indicators computed over the evaluation set (higher percentile indicates larger uncertainty). We also report consistency-based baselines (e.g., self-consistency, SC) when available. Our goal is not to show that AU and EU are uncorrelated, but that they respond to different sources of uncertainty.

G.1 Three signature regimes

Table 32 groups representative TruthfulQA cases into three regimes that match the intended semantics of the AU/EU split. (a) AU →\to ambiguity: open-ended or weakly-constrained inputs where repeated decoding yields high semantic dispersion (high AU) but intent-preserving paraphrases leave the semantic mean roughly fixed (low EU). (b) EU →\to knowledge sensitivity: the model is stable under repeated decoding (low AU) but paraphrases expose substantial drift (high EU); factual gaps, misconceptions, or brittle heuristics produce a confidently specific answer that small surface-form changes can flip. (c) Spurious determinism (Thm. 4.3): consistency-only scores collapse under deterministic decoding while EU stays high, exactly the regime where perturbations can succeed when consistency fails (SC≈\approx0 but UE≻0U_{E}{\succ}0).

G.2 Failure cases: when consistency baselines win

Theorem 4.3 gives a sufficient condition for perturbation advantage; in regimes where within-prompt decoding variability is the primary signal, consistency-only baselines remain competitive. Representative example: “How quickly will you be seen if brought by ambulance?” — model answers “Immediately” (GT: triage by priority); SC/SE rank this at percentile 9797 while AU/EU sit at 38/2138/21. Two patterns account for such failures: (i) the perturbation family does not explore the relevant decision boundary for that query (limited semantic coverage), so μΔ​(x)\mu_{\Delta}(x) does not vary; or (ii) the error is driven mainly by decoding randomness at a fixed prompt, the regime where SC/SE are designed to win.

Appendix H Experimental Settings

Tasks and datasets. We evaluate black-box uncertainty estimation on five QA benchmarks: TriviaQA (no-context) [21], TruthfulQA [31], GPQA [46], SciQA [3], and CoQA [44], with the goal of testing whether uncertainty can reliably predict answer correctness (§5). This follows the main experimental protocol in Sec. 5.

Models. We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs: meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct, meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [15, 43]. Unless otherwise stated, we use M=20M{=}20 inner samples and N=20N{=}20 outer perturbations (when applicable), consistent with §5.1.

Prompting and formatting. For all models, we use the official chat template provided by the tokenizer (apply_chat_template) to ensure consistent formatting across LLaMA and Qwen families. The user message is fixed as:

Answer the following question with only the short, direct answer and nothing else.
If you are unsure, reply with "I don’t know."
Avoid explanations or extra conversation.
Question: [QUESTION]
Answer:

The same instruction is applied to both the original and perturbed/paraphrased questions. Generated text is post-processed by stripping the prompt prefix to isolate the answer segment.

Correctness labeling. We use two complementary automatic criteria (§5.1): (1) Cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of generated vs. reference answers (threshold >0.8>0.8), and (2) ROUGE-L overlap (threshold >0.5>0.5) [45, 30]. We report results under both criteria to reduce metric-specific artifacts.

Evaluation metric (AUROC) and score convention. We report AUROC for correctness prediction under the standard UQ convention: incorrect is the positive class and the scoring signal is the (uncorrected sign) uncertainty value 𝒰⁡(x)\mathcal{U}(x) (AU, EU, or TU). AUROC then measures how well higher uncertainty ranks errors above correct answers. This convention is equivalent (same numeric AUROC) to taking correct as the positive class with score −𝒰⁡(x)-\mathcal{U}(x), and we do not switch between the two anywhere in the paper.

Computing infrastructure and software. Unless stated otherwise, experiments are run on a remote Linux cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40 GB) and multi-core CPUs. The environment uses Conda on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS with Python 3.10 and PyTorch/Transformers toolchains (full package list below).

Software Configuration:

  • •

    OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS

  • •

    Python: 3.10.18

  • •

    DL: PyTorch 2.6.0 (CUDA 12.1, cuDNN 9.1.0), TorchVision 0.19.0, TorchAudio 2.5.1

  • •

    NLP: Transformers 4.53.1, Sentence-Transformers 5.0.0, Accelerate 1.8.1

  • •

    Data/Utils: Datasets 4.0.0, NumPy 2.1.2, Pandas 2.3.1, SciPy 1.15.3, scikit-learn 1.7.0

  • •

    Other: HuggingFace Hub 0.33.2, TQDM 4.67.1, SentencePiece 0.2.0

H.1 Two-Level Ensemble (Ours)

The implementation matches Sec. 3 of the main paper; hyperparameters are in Table 33, and Algorithm 1 below gives the precise pseudocode corresponding to the visual pipeline in main-paper Fig. 1. We L2-normalize embeddings before covariance computation. Inner decoding uses do_sample=True with the parameters in Table 33 (matched to all sampling-based baselines for fair comparison); the greedy reference answer uses do_sample=False, num_beams=1.

Cost. N​MNM LLM calls and NN nearest-neighbour lookups per input; the paraphrase pool is built once per dataset.

H.2 Baselines

Baseline set. We compare against black-box UQ baselines: D-SE [24], Self-Consistency [54], SIMBA [4], SelfCheckGPT [35], SPUQ [13], and a verbalized self-evaluation P(True) probe [22]. We also compare to white-box methods requiring token-level probabilities: G-NLL [1], PE/LN-PE [34], and SE/LN-SE [24, 11]. All methods use the same base prompt; methods requiring auxiliary outputs (e.g., confidence verbalization) follow their original protocol while matching the generation budget as closely as possible.

Sampling for baselines (shared). For baseline methods that rely on multiple sampled generations, we generate S=10S{=}10 samples using: do_sample=True, num_return_sequences=10, top_k=50, top_p=0.99, temperature=0.9, and max_new_tokens=50, with pad_token_id=eos_token_id. The greedy reference answer uses do_sample=False, num_beams=1, and max_new_tokens=50.

Token-probability baselines (white-box). G-NLL [1]: NLL of the greedy answer under teacher forcing, loss restricted to answer tokens. PE: entropy of the categorical distribution formed by normalizing the SS sampled-answer sequence log-probabilities. LN-PE [34]: 1S​∑sNLLs/Ls\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s}\mathrm{NLL}_{s}/L_{s} with LsL_{s} the token count. SE [24, 11]: cluster the SS samples by bidirectional NLI entailment (DeBERTa-large; a,ba,b joined iff entailment in both directions), set cluster probabilities by summing per-sample sequence log-probabilities, score by cluster-distribution entropy. LN-SE: same as SE but length-normalize per-sample probabilities first.

Black-box baselines. D-SE [24]: SE with discrete cluster probabilities (frequency / SS), no token-level probabilities required. SC [54]: 1−maxc⁡|Cc|/S1-\max_{c}|C_{c}|/S over the same NLI clusters. SIMBA [4]: 1−sim¯1-\bar{\mathrm{sim}}, the mean pairwise cosine similarity among the SS sampled-answer embeddings. SelfCheckGPT [35]: canonical BERTScore variant; for each spaCy sentence rir_{i} in the greedy answer, u⁡(ri)=1−maxn⁡BERTScore⁡(ri,Sn)u(r_{i}){=}1{-}\max_{n}\mathrm{BERTScore}(r_{i},S_{n}) (RoBERTa-large F1), aggregated by mean. SPUQ [13]: KSPUQ=10K_{\mathrm{SPUQ}}{=}10 perturbed prompts via the three SPUQ modes (paraphrase, dummy-token, system-message), one decode each; score 1−r¯1{-}\bar{r} with r¯\bar{r} the mean pairwise ROUGE-L; closest perturbation-based comparator (App. D). P(True) probe [22]: post-hoc “Is the answer above correct? Yes/No”; Yes↦0\mapsto 0, No↦1\mapsto 1, ambiguous ↦0.5\mapsto 0.5. We do not implement the trained-verbalization protocol of Lin et al. [32] (not zero-shot black-box).

Post-processing. We consistently strip the chat-formatted prompt prefix to obtain the answer text. Empty answers are treated as length 11 when computing length-normalized metrics to avoid division by zero.

Notes on ensemble sizes and covariance summaries. The inner size MM controls within-input variability (aleatoric estimation) and the outer size NN controls perturbation diversity (epistemic estimation); we use M=N=20M{=}N{=}20 unless otherwise stated. For scalar summaries of embedding covariances, we use trace⁡(Σ)\mathrm{trace}(\Sigma) (other options like det(Σ)\det(\Sigma), or largest eigenvalues are also valid).

Appendix I Detailed Limitations Analysis

This section expands on the limitations summarized in Sec. 6 (L1–L5), detailing the underlying assumptions, potential failure modes, and empirical scope of our framework.

I.1 L1: Surrogate target and local bridge assumptions

Because the parameter posterior p⁡(θ∣𝒟)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{D}) is intractable and inaccessible in black-box LLM deployment, our estimator does not directly measure Bayesian parameter uncertainty. Instead, it targets perturbation-population AU and EU at fixed model weights θ⋆\theta^{\star}, using input perturbations pΔp_{\Delta} as an observational proxy for epistemic variation. This introduces two fundamental limitations:

  • •

    Dependence on perturbation design: As in general statistical variance decompositions [9, 56], the operational quantities (UA,UE)(U_{A},U_{E}) are defined relative to the chosen perturbation distribution pΔp_{\Delta} and decoding temperature (App. F.2.1); changing the perturbation radius or paraphrase generator changes the scale of UEU_{E}.

  • •

    Violation of local bridge conditions: Our theoretical bound linking perturbation EU to Bayesian parameter EU (Thm. 4.2) relies on three local conditions: first-order linearity of the conditional embedding mean (D1\mathrm{D1}), local Gaussianity of the predictive distribution (D2\mathrm{D2}), and directional coverage of parameter-induced shifts by input perturbations (D3\mathrm{D3}). When these assumptions fail—for instance, if a model is uniformly overconfident in a false belief across an entire paraphrase neighborhood—perturbation variance collapses even though true epistemic error remains high.

To help detect when the local approximation breaks down, Sec. 4.2 (Tab. 12) introduces data-estimable diagnostics (D1\mathrm{D1}–D3\mathrm{D3}), though we note that the multivariate normality test (D2\mathrm{D2}) has limited statistical power at small inner sample sizes (M=10M{=}10) in high-dimensional embedding spaces (d=384d{=}384).

I.2 L2: Imperfect paraphrase generation and semantic drift

The law-of-total-covariance decomposition assumes that outer perturbations xΔ∼pΔ(⋅∣x)x_{\Delta}\sim p_{\Delta}(\cdot\mid x) strictly preserve the task semantics of the original query xx. In practice, off-the-shelf LLM paraphrase generators frequently introduce semantic drift, such as dropping qualifying constraints, altering named entities, flipping polarity, or shifting question specificity. When a generated rewrite changes the underlying question, the resulting shift in predictive embeddings reflects task shift rather than epistemic uncertainty about xx, spuriously inflating UEU_{E} and blurring the boundary between AU and EU. In our human audit of raw generated paraphrases (App. F.2.3), approximately 40%40\% of candidate rewrites failed at least one strict semantic-equivalence criterion. Although our sensitivity experiments on TriviaQA show that moderate paraphrase noise has a bounded effect on aggregate AUROC and rank correlations (Tab. 25), deploying the method reliably on complex or constraint-heavy prompts requires pairing paraphrase generation with automated NLI or LLM-based semantic filtering.

I.3 L3: Representation dependence on the sentence encoder

Because predictive variability is computed in the representation space of an external encoder e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot), both UAU_{A} and UEU_{E} are joint properties of the LLM and the embedding map. Relying on a fixed sentence encoder introduces two limitations:

  • •

    Encoder blind spots and geometric bias: Off-the-shelf sentence encoders trained for general semantic similarity can be insensitive to fine-grained factual contradictions, antonym flips, or numerical discrepancies that share high lexical overlap, causing e⁡(y)e(y) to understate true semantic disagreement. Conversely, stylistic or structural variations in surface form may be mapped to distant embeddings even when the underlying factual answers agree.

  • •

    Lack of cross-encoder calibration: Because trace and log-determinant magnitudes scale with the dimensionality and geometry of e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot), absolute uncertainty scores are not directly comparable across different encoders.

We evaluate sensitivity across three general-purpose encoders (SBERT, MPNet, and BGE-base) in Tab. 7(a) and App. F.5 (Tabs. 28–29), where relative per-example rankings remain stable (ρ≥0.955\rho\geq 0.955) despite shifts in absolute scale. Nevertheless, specialized domains such as mathematical reasoning, code generation, or clinical text may require domain-specific encoders or task-adapted similarity metrics.

I.4 L4: Computational overhead of nested sampling

Estimating both within-perturbation and between-perturbation covariances via nested Monte Carlo requires N×MN\times M autoregressive generations per query (e.g., 100100–400400 decodes in our standard configurations), plus constructing an offline paraphrase pool of size KpoolK_{\mathrm{pool}}. This is an order of magnitude more expensive in token generation and wall-clock latency than single-pass white-box estimators or one-level black-box consistency baselines (which typically use 55–2020 generations), making full nested sampling prohibitive for strict low-latency or high-throughput online serving. Furthermore, when constrained to a small, strictly matched generation budget B=N​MB=NM (e.g., B=20B{=}20), dividing samples across two hierarchy levels increases estimation variance per level and does not improve raw error-ranking AUROC over leading one-level baselines (Sec. 5.3, Tab. 2). While budget ablations (Tabs. 18–30) and variance-based adaptive stopping (which reduces median cost to 2525 decodes in App. F.1.2) mitigate overhead, reducing the sample complexity of two-level black-box UQ remains an open challenge.

I.5 L5: Scope of empirical tasks and interventional validation

Our empirical evaluation is subject to two scope limitations:

  • •

    Focus on short-form QA: Aside from a small-scale claim-level pilot on 5050 NQ queries (Sec. 5.6), our experiments focus on short-form question answering where response equivalence is well captured by sentence embeddings. Scaling nested covariance decomposition to long-form open-ended generation, multi-step reasoning traces, or interactive agent trajectories is non-trivial, as responses vary simultaneously in length, discourse structure, and set-level claim composition.

  • •

    Simplified single-factor interventions: Our paired-intervention benchmark tests two clean, synthetic manipulations: (1) resolving prompt ambiguity on AmbigQA and (2) injecting gold supporting passages on NQ and conducts the standardized score-shift comparison against baselines on a single backbone (LLaMA-3-8B; Tab. 5). In realistic RAG or multi-turn deployments, uncertainty sources rarely occur in isolation: retrieved passages may be noisy, partially relevant, or internally contradictory, causing aleatoric and epistemic effects to interact in ways not captured by single-factor interventions.

I.6 Broader impact

Decomposing predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components can improve the reliability of deployed LLM systems by informing targeted actions, such as asking clarifying questions under high AU or invoking retrieval and abstention under high EU in high-stakes domains. At the same time, because the decomposition relies on surrogate perturbations and embedding representations, treating empirical AU/EU estimates as formal guarantees could lead to misplaced trust or inappropriate routing when bridge conditions or paraphrase validity fail. Finally, nested Monte Carlo sampling substantially increases inference-time compute and energy consumption if deployed at scale without adaptive stopping or selective triggering.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction clearly state the theoretical and empirical contributions and their scope, including the local diagnostic conditions of the Bayesian bridge (Sec. 4.2) and the matched-budget comparison (Sec. 5.3).

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: See Sec. 6 and App. I.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

    Experimental result reproducibility

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: We only release research code for the proposed method and its evaluation, which does not pose a significant risk of misuse.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: All datasets and models used are publicly released and properly cited; see App. H.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The released code is documented in the public repository at https://github.com/wma17/Black-box_UQ_for_LLMs_Ensemble_of_Ensemble, including implementation details, usage instructions, dependencies, and licensing information.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The authors themselves annotated 100 model-generated question pairs using a blind evaluation form (App. F.2.3). No external annotators or crowdsourcing participants were recruited.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: The annotation task involved only co-authors evaluating model-generated text. No external human participants were recruited, and no personal or behavioral data about the annotators were collected.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

  76. 16.

    Declaration of LLM usage

  77. Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  79. Justification: LLMs are the primary subjects of study and evaluation. We also use standard LLM-based evaluation procedures, including an LLM grader for perturbation checks (App. F.2.3) and LLM-based claim extraction and factuality assessment (App. E). These procedures are described in the paper. LLMs were also used for editing and for help implementing standard methods.

  80. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components.

    • •

      Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
